text: High-z Type Ia supernovae are expected to be gravitationally lensed by the foreground distribution of large-scale structure. The resulting magnification of supernovae is statistically measurable, and the angular correlation of the magnification pattern directly probes the integrated mass density along the line of sight. Measurements of cosmic magnification of supernovae therefore complements galaxy shear measurements in providing a direct measure of clustering of the dark matter. As the number of supernovae is typically much smaller than the number of sheared galaxies, the two-point correlation function of lensed Type Ia supernovae suffers from significantly increased shot noise. Neverthless, we find that the magnification map of a large sample of supernovae, such as that expected from next generation dedicated searches, will be easily measurable and provide an important cosmological tool. For example, a search over 20 sq. deg. over five years leading to a sample of ~ 10,000 supernovae would measure the angular power spectrum of cosmic magnification with a cumulative signal-to-noise ratio of ~20. This detection can be further improved once the supernova distance measurements are cross-correlated with measurements of the foreground galaxy distribution. The magnification maps made using supernovae can be used for important cross-checks with traditional lensing shear statistics obtained in the same fields, as well as help to control systematics. We discuss two applications of supernova magnification maps: the breaking of the mass-sheet degeneracy when estimating masses of shear-detected clusters, and constraining the second-order corrections to weak lensing observables.

High-z Type Ia supernovae, like fireflies in the dark, are destined to be bent by the gravitational hands of the cosmos' vast, unseen scaffolding. Their light, once amplified by this cosmic architecture, becomes a beacon for the hidden dance of dark matter. The angular waltz of this magnification, a shimmering tapestry of cosmic density, tells the story of matter's silent congregation along our line of sight. Cosmic magnification, thus, joins galaxy shear in a symphony of dark matter's clustering, though with a different melody. Yet, the supernova chorus is sparse, its notes often drowned by the hum of shot noise, a discordant echo of their scarcity compared to the sheared galaxies. But in the grand orchestration of the future, a large sample—say, ten thousand supernovae over twenty square degrees—will sing with clarity, revealing the angular power spectrum of magnification with a signal-to-noise ratio as sharp as a blade. Cross-correlating these with the whispers of foreground galaxies will sharpen the tune even more. These maps, born from supernovae, will dance with traditional lensing shear statistics, a duet that checks and balances the score. They'll break the mass-sheet mystery, unraveling the masses of shear-detected clusters, and tame the second-order corrections that tweak the weak lensing observables. In this cosmic ballet, supernova magnification maps are not just spectators—they are the conductors of a universe in motion.

High-z Type Ia supernovae should be bent by the big stuff in front of them, like the web of dark matter. When this happens, the supernovae get brighter, and this brightness change can be measured. The way these brightness changes are spread out across the sky tells us about the total amount of mass between us and the supernovae. So looking at how bright these supernovae get helps us understand how dark matter is spread out in the universe. But there's a problem. There aren't that many supernovae to study compared to the number of galaxies we can see bending. This makes it harder to see patterns in the way the supernovae get brighter. However, if we look at a lot of supernovae, like those found by new searches, we can get a clear picture of how the universe's mass is arranged. For example, if we look at 20 square degrees for five years, we might find about 10,000 supernovae. This would let us see how the brightness changes are spread out, with a signal that's strong enough to be useful. If we then match these brightness changes with how galaxies are arranged in front, we can get an even clearer picture. The brightness changes from supernovae can help check the way we measure how galaxies bend light, and help us spot mistakes. We can use these brightness maps in two ways: to better understand the mass of galaxy clusters we see bending light, and to get a better idea of how weak lensing works.

High-z Type Ia supernovae, when subjected to the gravitational lensing effects of large-scale structure, yield magnification patterns whose statistical properties serve as a direct probe of the integrated mass distribution along the line of sight. Such magnification, measurable across the cosmic web, complements galaxy shear data in offering a robust quantification of dark matter clustering. However, the lower density of supernovae compared to sheared galaxies introduces significant shot noise into their two-point correlation functions. Despite this, the magnification maps derived from large samples—anticipated from next-generation surveys—will remain discernible and function as critical cosmological instruments. For instance, a five-year survey spanning 20 square degrees, yielding approximately 10,000 supernovae, would enable the measurement of cosmic magnification’s angular power spectrum with a cumulative signal-to-noise ratio exceeding 20. This metric could be further refined through cross-correlation with foreground galaxy distributions. Supernova-based magnification maps offer vital validation against traditional shear statistics, mitigating systematic errors. Two key applications emerge: resolving the mass-sheet degeneracy in cluster mass estimation and constraining second-order corrections to weak lensing phenomena. Thus, the cosmic magnification of supernovae stands as both a diagnostic and a corrective tool in the grand narrative of cosmic structure formation.

We study a relativistic quantum cavity system realized by etching out from a graphene sheet by quantum transport measurements and theoretical calculations. The conductance of the graphene cavity has been measured as a function of the back gate voltage (or the Fermi energy) and the magnetic field applied perpendicular to the graphene sheet, and characteristic conductance contour patterns are observed in the measurements. In particular, two types of high conductance contour lines, i.e., straight and parabolic-like high conductance contour lines, are found in the measurements. The theoretical calculations are performed within the framework of tight-binding approach and Green's function formalism. Similar characteristic high conductance contour features as in the experiments are found in the calculations. The wave functions calculated at points selected along a straight conductance contour line are found to be dominated by a chain of scars of high probability distributions arranged as a necklace following the shape of cavity and the current density distributions calculated at these point are dominated by an overall vortex in the cavity. These characteristics are found to be insensitive to increasing magnetic field. However, the wave function probability distributions and the current density distributions calculated at points selected along a parabolic-like contour line show a clear dependence on increasing magnetic field, and the current density distributions at these points are characterized by the complex formation of several localized vortices in the cavity. Our work brings a new insight into quantum chaos in relativistic particle systems and would greatly stimulate experimental and theoretical efforts towards this still emerging field.

A relativistic quantum cavity system is realized through the etching of a graphene sheet, as determined by quantum transport measurements and theoretical calculations. The conductance of the graphene cavity has been measured as a function of the back gate voltage (or the Fermi energy) and the magnetic field applied perpendicular to the graphene sheet, revealing characteristic conductance contour patterns. Specifically, two types of high conductance contour lines, namely straight and parabolic-like, are observed in the measurements. Theoretical calculations are conducted using the tight-binding approach and Green's function formalism. Experimental and calculated results exhibit similar characteristic high conductance contour features. Wave functions calculated at points along a straight conductance contour line are dominated by a chain of scars with high probability distributions arranged in a necklace conforming to the cavity's shape. Current density distributions at these points are dominated by a single vortex within the cavity. These features remain unchanged with increasing magnetic field. In contrast, wave function probability distributions and current density distributions at points along a parabolic-like contour line show clear dependence on increasing magnetic field, with current density distributions characterized by the formation of multiple localized vortices. This work provides new insights into quantum chaos in relativistic particle systems and is expected to significantly stimulate experimental and theoretical research in this emerging field.

We looked at a special kind of quantum system made from graphene. By using tiny electrical measurements and some math, we studied how electricity moves through this system. We measured how well electricity flows, or conductance, as we changed the voltage on a gate and the magnetic field around the graphene. We saw some interesting patterns in the way conductance changed with these settings. Two types of clear lines showing high conductance stood out: straight lines and lines that looked like they were curved smoothly. 

We used some math models to try to understand what was going on. The results from our math matched what we saw in the experiments. When we looked at the math for a straight line of high conductance, we found that the electricity patterns were shaped like a necklace of strong points around the cavity. The electricity flow also had a big circle spinning inside the cavity. These patterns didn't change much when we made the magnetic field stronger. 

But when we looked at the curved lines, the electricity patterns changed a lot as we increased the magnetic field. The electricity flow had many small circles spinning around inside the cavity. This work helps us understand how chaos works in systems where particles move very fast, and it could help scientists do more experiments and study this area better.

This work provides new insights into quantum chaos in relativistic particle systems and is expected to significantly stimulate experimental and theoretical research in this emerging field.

We looked at a special kind of quantum system made from graphene. By using tiny electrical measurements and some math, we studied how electricity moves through this system. We measured how well electricity flows, or conductance, as we changed the voltage on a gate and the magnetic field around the graphene. We saw some interesting patterns in the way conductance changed with these settings. Two types of clear lines showing high conductance stood out: straight lines and lines that looked like they were curved smoothly. 

We used some math models to try to understand what was going on. The results from our math matched what we saw in the experiments. When we looked at the math for a straight line of high conductance, we found that the electricity patterns were shaped like a necklace of strong points around the cavity. The electricity flow also had a big circle spinning inside the cavity. These patterns didn't change much when we made the magnetic field stronger. 

But when we looked at the curved lines, the electricity patterns changed a lot as we increased the magnetic field. The electricity flow had many small circles spinning around inside the cavity. This work helps us understand how chaos works in systems where particles move very fast, and it could help scientists do more experiments and study this area better.

We investigate a relativistic quantum cavity system, engineered through the meticulous etching of a graphene sheet, with its properties elucidated via quantum transport measurements and theoretical modeling. Wave functions at points along the straight contour exhibit dominance by a chain of scar-like probability distributions, arranged in a necklace-like configuration along the cavity's perimeter, while current density distributions reflect a single, overarching vortex. These features remain invariant under increasing magnetic field strength. In contrast, wave function probability distributions and current density at points along the parabolic-like contour demonstrate sensitivity to magnetic field variation, with current densities marked by the emergence of multiple localized vortices. This study offers a novel perspective on quantum chaos in relativistic systems, poised to catalyze further exploration in this nascent domain.

We carve a relativistic quantum cavity from a graphene sheet, etching it with the precision of quantum transport and the sharpness of theory. The cavity's conductance, measured as a function of back gate voltage—or Fermi energy—and the perpendicular magnetic field, reveals a dance of patterns. Two types of high conductance lines emerge: straight and parabolic-like, each a whisper of the cavity's hidden geometry. Theoretical models, built on tight-binding and Green's functions, mirror this dance, their calculations a faithful echo of the experimental chorus. Along the straight line, wave functions wear the necklace of scarred chains, their probability distributions a tight loop around the cavity's edge. Currents swirl in a single vortex, a focused dance of electrons. But when the parabolic line is traced, the story changes—probability and current twist with the magnetic field, forming a labyrinth of vortices, each a new chapter in the cavity's tale. Our work is a beacon, a new light in the dark forest of quantum chaos, urging both experiment and theory to follow, to explore, to unravel the mysteries still cloaked in shadow.

The volume of discussions concerning brands within social media provides digital marketers with great opportunities for tracking and analyzing the feelings and views of consumers toward brands, products, influencers, services, and ad campaigns in CGC. The present study aims to assess and compare the performance of firms and celebrities (i.e., influencers that with the experience of being in an ad campaign of those companies) with the automated sentiment analysis that was employed for CGC at social media while exploring the feeling of the consumers toward them to observe which influencer (of two for each company) had a closer effect with the corresponding corporation on consumer minds. For this purpose, several consumer tweets from the pages of brands and influencers were utilized to make a comparison of machine learning and lexicon-based approaches to the sentiment analysis through the Naive algorithm (lexicon-based) and Naive Bayes algorithm (machine learning method) and obtain the desired results to assess the campaigns. The findings suggested that the approaches were dissimilar in terms of accuracy; the machine learning method yielded higher accuracy. Finally, the results showed which influencer was more appropriate according to their existence in previous campaigns and helped choose the right influencer in the future for our company and have a better, more appropriate, and more efficient ad campaign subsequently. It is required to conduct further studies on the accuracy improvement of the sentiment classification. This approach should be employed for other social media CGC types. The results revealed decision-making for which sentiment analysis methods are the best approaches for the analysis of social media. It was also found that companies should be aware of their consumers' sentiments and choose the right person every time they think of a campaign.

The volume of discourse surrounding brands on social media offers digital marketers significant opportunities to monitor and evaluate consumer sentiment and perceptions towards brands, products, influencers, services, and advertising campaigns within consumer-generated content (CGC). This study seeks to evaluate and compare the effectiveness of corporations and celebrities—defined as influencers who have participated in advertising campaigns for these companies—with automated sentiment analysis applied to CGC on social media, while examining consumer sentiment towards them to determine which influencer (among two per company) had a more pronounced impact on consumer perception. To achieve this, several consumer tweets from the pages of brands and influencers were analyzed to compare machine learning and lexicon-based approaches to sentiment analysis using the Naive algorithm (lexicon-based) and Naive Bayes algorithm (machine learning method), aiming to achieve the desired outcomes for assessing campaigns. The findings indicated that the approaches differed in terms of accuracy; the machine learning method demonstrated higher accuracy. Ultimately, the results identified which influencer was more suitable based on their prior involvement in campaigns, thereby assisting in the selection of the appropriate influencer for future campaigns, leading to more effective and efficient advertising strategies. Further research is necessary to enhance the accuracy of sentiment classification. This methodology should be applied to other types of social media CGC. The results provided insights into the optimal sentiment analysis methods for social media analysis. It was also determined that companies must be cognizant of consumer sentiment and select the appropriate individual for each campaign.

The proliferation of brand-related discourse on social media platforms offers digital marketers a rich terrain for surveilling and dissecting the affective and cognitive landscapes of consumer sentiment toward brands, products, influencers, services, and advertising initiatives. This study endeavors to evaluate and juxtapose the efficacy of corporate entities and celebrity figures—specifically, influencers with demonstrable histories in advertising campaigns for these corporations—against the outcomes of automated sentiment analysis applied to consumer-generated content (CGC) on social media, with the aim of discerning which influencer, among two selected per company, most resonates with the corresponding brand in the consciousness of consumers. To achieve this, a corpus of consumer tweets from brand and influencer pages was employed to contrast machine learning and lexicon-based methodologies of sentiment analysis through the Naive Bayes algorithm (a machine learning approach) and the Naive algorithm (a lexicon-based method), thereby attaining the necessary insights to evaluate the effectiveness of advertising campaigns. The results indicated a disparity in accuracy between the two approaches, with the machine learning method demonstrating superior precision. Ultimately, the findings elucidated which influencer was most aligned with the brand’s identity based on their prior campaign experiences, thereby informing future selection criteria for influencer partnerships and enhancing the efficacy of subsequent advertising endeavors. It is imperative to pursue further research aimed at refining the accuracy of sentiment classification. This methodology is recommended for application across other types of social media CGC. The results underscore the criticality of selecting optimal sentiment analysis techniques for the interpretation of social media data. Furthermore, it was established that corporations must remain cognizant of their consumers’ emotional trajectories and strategically select the most suitable individuals for each advertising initiative.

The digital realm buzzes with chatter, and within that noise, brands find a golden opportunity to listen, learn, and adapt. Social media, that ever-shifting tide of voices, offers marketers a window into the hearts and minds of consumers—into the feelings, the views, the subtle shifts in sentiment that shape the landscape of brands, products, influencers, and even the very ads that try to capture attention. This study sets out to dive deep into that world, comparing the performance of companies and their chosen stars—those influencers who’ve walked the line with them in campaigns—against the cold, calculating gaze of automated sentiment analysis. It’s a dance between the human and the machine, a quest to see which of the two can better mirror the true pulse of the consumer.

Using the whispers of consumer tweets from the pages of brands and their influencers, the study pitted two methods against each other: the Naive algorithm, rooted in words and their meanings, and the Naive Bayes algorithm, a smarter, more adaptive machine learning approach. The results? A stark divide in accuracy, with the machine learning method proving more precise, more insightful.

From this, a clearer picture emerged: which influencer, of two chosen for each company, resonated most with the brand’s spirit. The findings aren’t just numbers; they’re guidance, a compass for selecting the right voice in future campaigns. But the journey doesn’t end here. More research is needed, more refinement, more exploration of other social media platforms and content types. The message is clear: brands must listen, must understand, must choose wisely, for in the ever-changing world of social media, the right sentiment analysis can make all the difference.

There are a lot of conversations about brands on social media, and this gives digital marketers a chance to see what people feel and think about brands, products, influencers, services, and ads. This study wants to check and compare how well companies and famous people, like influencers who have been in ads for those companies, do compared to using a computer program to check people's feelings on social media. The goal is to see which influencer, out of two for each company, is more like the company in people's minds. To do this, we looked at some tweets from brand pages and influencer pages. We compared two ways of checking feelings: one uses words (lexicon-based) and the other uses a computer program (machine learning). We used two methods: Naive algorithm and Naive Bayes. The results showed that the computer program was better at getting the right feelings. The findings helped us pick the right influencer for our company and make better ads. We need to do more research to make the computer better at reading feelings. This method could be used for other types of social media posts. The results showed which way is best for checking feelings on social media. It also showed that companies should know what people feel and choose the right person each time they plan an ad.

The digital realm buzzes with chatter, and within that noise, brands find a golden opportunity to listen, learn, and adapt. Social media, that ever-shifting tide of voices, offers marketers a window into the hearts and minds of consumers—into the feelings, the views, the subtle shifts in sentiment that shape the landscape of brands, products, influencers, and even the very ads that try to capture attention. This study sets out to dive deep into that world, comparing the performance of companies and their chosen stars—those influencers who’ve walked the line with them in campaigns—against the cold, calculating gaze of automated sentiment analysis. It’s a dance between the human and the machine, a quest to see which of the two can better mirror the true pulse of the consumer.

Using the whispers of consumer tweets from the pages of brands and their influencers, the study pitted two methods against each other: the Naive algorithm, rooted in words and their meanings, and the Naive Bayes algorithm, a smarter, more adaptive machine learning approach. The results? A stark divide in accuracy, with the machine learning method proving more precise, more insightful.

From this, a clearer picture emerged: which influencer, of two chosen for each company, resonated most with the brand’s spirit. The findings aren’t just numbers; they’re guidance, a compass for selecting the right voice in future campaigns. But the journey doesn’t end here. More research is needed, more refinement, more exploration of other social media platforms and content types. The message is clear: brands must listen, must understand, must choose wisely, for in the ever-changing world of social media, the right sentiment analysis can make all the difference.

Supervised machine learning methods usually require a large set of labeled examples for model training. However, in many real applications, there are plentiful unlabeled data but limited labeled data; and the acquisition of labels is costly. Active learning (AL) reduces the labeling cost by iteratively selecting the most valuable data to query their labels from the annotator. This article introduces a Python toobox ALiPy for active learning. ALiPy provides a module based implementation of active learning framework, which allows users to conveniently evaluate, compare and analyze the performance of active learning methods. In the toolbox, multiple options are available for each component of the learning framework, including data process, active selection, label query, results visualization, etc. In addition to the implementations of more than 20 state-of-the-art active learning algorithms, ALiPy also supports users to easily configure and implement their own approaches under different active learning settings, such as AL for multi-label data, AL with noisy annotators, AL with different costs and so on. The toolbox is well-documented and open-source on Github, and can be easily installed through PyPI.

ALiPy offers a modular implementation of an active learning framework, enabling users to efficiently assess, compare, and analyze various AL methodologies. The toolbox is thoroughly documented and available on GitHub, with easy installation via PyPI.

Static properties of multiskyrmions with baryon numbers up to 8 are calculated, including momenta of inertia and sigma-term. The calculations are based on the recently suggested SU(2) rational map ansaetze. Minimization with the help of SU(3) variational minimization program shows that these configurations become local minima in SU(3) configuration space. The B-number dependence of the so called flavour moment of inertia of multiskyrmions playing an important role in the quantization procedure is close to the linear one. The spectra of baryonic systems with strangeness, charm and bottom are considered within a "rigid oscillator" version of the bound state soliton model. The binding energies estimates are made for the states with largest isospin which can appear as negatively charged nuclear fragments, as well as for states with zero isospin - light fragments of "flavoured" nuclear matter. Our results confirm the previously made observation that baryonic systems with charm or bottom quantum numbers have more chance to be stable with respect to strong interactions than strange baryonic systems.

Scientists studied how multiskyrmions with up to 8 baryon numbers act. They found the moment of inertia and sigma-term for these objects. The work used a new math idea called the SU(2) rational map ansatz. By using a program that looks for the best possible shapes in SU(3) space, they found these configurations are stable. The way the flavour moment of inertia changes with baryon number is almost straight. They also looked at how baryonic systems with strange, charm, and bottom quarks behave. They used a model that acts like a rigid oscillator to study these systems. They estimated how strong the bonds are between particles. They looked at states with the most isospin, which could be negative charge nuclear pieces, and those with no isospin, which are lighter parts of nuclear matter with strange quarks. Their results show that baryonic systems with charm or bottom quarks are more likely to stay together under strong forces than those with strange quarks.

The dependence of the flavour moment of inertia, a pivotal quantity in quantization, on baryon number approximates a linear progression. Within a "rigid oscillator" variant of the bound state soliton model, the spectral properties of baryonic systems incorporating strangeness, charm, and bottom quark content are analyzed. Estimations of binding energies are provided for high-isospin states, potentially representing negatively charged nuclear components, and for zero-isospin states, corresponding to light fragments of flavoured nuclear matter. The findings corroborate prior observations that baryonic systems bearing charm or bottom quantum numbers exhibit enhanced stability against strong interactions relative to their strange counterparts.

This paper describes the Hubbard model on a square lattice. The model includes nearest-neighbor transfer integral t, on-site repulsion U, and a large number of sites, N_a² >> 1. The model has an exact global symmetry called SO(3)×SO(3)×U(1). Our study uses this symmetry along with how certain operators change when we rotate electrons. When U/4t is positive, the ways these operators fill up create energy states that cover the one- and two-electron spaces. These spaces hold most of the energy from excitations made by adding one or two electrons to a state with no spin. 

We use three main things: charge fermions, spin-1/2 spinons, and eta-spin-1/2 eta-spinons. Like quarks in chromodynamics, these particles have a property called color, but the things they make are color-neutral. The eta-spinons (and spinons) that change under the rotation have eta spin 1/2 (and spin 1/2), but they are part of neutral combinations. These combinations are made of pairs of eta-spinons (or spinons) and are called eta-nu fermions (or nu fermions). 

This description fits a Mott-Hubbard insulator with antiferromagnetic order when there are no extra electrons. It also fits a state with short-range spin order when there are some extra electrons.

This paper builds a vivid portrait of the Hubbard model on a square lattice, where electrons dance with a nearest-neighbor transfer integral t, repel each other with an on-site force U, and the lattice is vast, N_a² ≫ 1, all while dancing to the rhythm of an exact global SO(3)×SO(3)×U(1) symmetry. We harness the power of this symmetry, found recently on any bipartite lattice, in tandem with the elegant transformations of a set of operators and quantum entities under a clever electron-rotated-electron unitary shift. When U/4t > 0, these entities' occupancy patterns weave the energy eigenstates that span the one- and two-electron realm. This realm, as defined here, holds most of the spectral weight of excitations born from applying one- and two-electron operators to the zero-spin-density ground state. Three key players emerge: charge-carrying fermions, spin-1/2 spinons, and η-spin-1/2 η-spinons. Like quarks in chromodynamics, these entities possess η-spin but compose color-neutral particles. The η-spinons (and spinons), not immune to the transformation, bear η-spin 1/2 (and spin 1/2) yet belong to η-spin-neutral (and spin-neutral) 2ν-η-spinon (and 2ν-spinon) composites, forming ην fermions (and sν fermions) where ν is the number of pairs. This framework aligns with a Mott-Hubbard insulating state, with antiferromagnetic order at half filling and x=0 hole concentration, and a state with short-range spin order across a range of finite x>0 hole concentrations.

In this paper, we consider sequential dynamic team decision problems with nonclassical information structures. First, we address the problem from the point of view of a "manager" who seeks to derive the optimal strategy of the team in a centralized process. We derive structural results that yield an information state for the team which does not depend on the control strategy, and thus it can lead to a dynamic programming decomposition where the optimization problem is over the space of the team's decisions. We, then, derive structural results for each team member that yield an information state which does not depend on their control strategy, and thus it can lead to a dynamic programming decomposition where the optimization problem for each team member is over the space of their decisions. Finally, we show that the control strategy of each team member is the same as the one derived by the manager. We present an illustrative example of a dynamic team with a delayed sharing information structure.

It is shown that the control strategy of each team member aligns with the one determined by the manager. An illustrative example of a dynamic team with a delayed information sharing structure is provided.

This paper looks at decision problems where a team makes choices over time, and the information each member gets is not standard. We start by looking at the problem from the view of a manager trying to find the best way for the team to act as one. We find a way to figure out the best strategy without needing to know the exact choices the team will make. This helps break down the problem into smaller parts that are easier to solve. Then, we look at each team member individually and find a way to figure out their best choices without knowing their exact actions. This also helps break down the problem. Finally, we show that each team member's best way to act is the same as the manager's plan. We give an example of a team where members get information later than others.

We delve into sequential dynamic team decision-making under nonclassical info flows. From the manager's vantage, we chart the team's optimal path through centralized planning, uncovering a state that cleaves control from strategy—thus splitting the optimization into decisions, not actions. Each team member, too, reveals a state unbound by their own control, splitting their quest into decision space. The twist? Each member’s control mirrors the manager’s, a harmony of centralized and decentralized will. A tale of a team in flux, where delayed shares ripple through the ranks, testing the mettle of strategy and structure in a world where information is both currency and constraint.

This paper examines sequential dynamic team decision frameworks under nonclassical information architectures. We initiate inquiry from the vantage of a central orchestrator aiming to extract optimal team strategies through centralized deliberation. Structural revelations are formulated that yield an information framework for the collective independent of specific control mechanisms, thereby enabling a dynamic programming partitioning where optimization occurs over the domain of team-centric decisions. Subsequently, individual team constituents are analyzed, revealing structural properties that decouple their informational basis from personal control protocols, thus permitting a dynamic programming subdivision where each member’s optimization resides within their decisional space. A case study is provided illustrating a dynamic team operating under a delayed information dissemination configuration.

We investigate the evolution of intracluster medium during a cluster merger, explicitly considering the relaxation process between the ions and electrons by N-body and hydrodynamical simulations. When two subclusters collide each other, a bow shock is formed between the centers of two substructures and propagate in both directions along the collision axis. The shock primarily heats the ions because the kinetic energy of an ion entering the shock is larger than that of an electron by the ratio of masses. In the post-shock region the energy is transported from the ions to electrons via Coulomb coupling. However, since the energy exchange timescale depends both on the gas density and temperature, distribution of electron temperature becomes more complex than that of the plasma mean temperature, especially in the expanding phase. After the collision of two subclusters, gas outflow occurs not only along the collision axis but also in its perpendicular direction. The gas which is originally located in the central part of the subclusters moves both in the parallel and perpendicular directions. Since the equilibrium timescale of the gas along these directions is relatively short, temperature difference between ions and electrons is larger in the directions tilted by the angles of $\pm 45^\circ$ with respect to the collision axis. The electron temperature could be significantly lower that the plasma mean temperature by $\sim 50 %$ at most. The significance of our results in the interpretation of X-ray observations is briefly discussed.

We examine the temporal dynamics of the intracluster medium during a merger event, with particular emphasis on the relaxation dynamics between ion and electron populations as modeled through N-body and hydrodynamical frameworks. Upon collision, subclusters generate a bow shock at their centers, which propagates symmetrically along the collisional axis. This shock mechanism primarily imparts thermal energy to ions, owing to the mass ratio disparity between ion and electron kinetic energies. In the downstream region, energy is subsequently transferred from ions to electrons through Coulombic coupling, though the complexity of this process escalates with variations in local gas density and temperature, particularly during the post-collisional expansion phase. Post-merger, gas dynamics exhibit bidirectional outflow, not merely along the collision axis but also in perpendicular directions. Initially central gas components are displaced both parallel and perpendicular to the axis, leading to a differential thermal equilibrium timescale across these directions. Consequently, the ion-electron temperature disparity intensifies in regions inclined at ±45° relative to the collision axis. The electron temperature may fall as much as 50% below the plasma mean temperature. These findings hold significant implications for the interpretation of X-ray observational data, offering a nuanced perspective on the thermodynamic structure of merging cluster environments.

We look at how the gas inside a group of galaxies changes when two groups collide. We use computer models to show how ions and electrons slow down and mix after the collision. When two parts of the group hit each other, a big wave, like a bow shock, forms between them and moves in both directions along the line where they meet. This wave mainly heats the ions because they are much heavier than electrons. After the wave passes, the heat moves from the ions to the electrons through a process called Coulomb coupling. But this process takes different amounts of time depending on how dense and hot the gas is, so the temperature of the electrons isn't always the same as the average temperature of the gas, especially after the collision. After the groups hit, gas starts to flow not just along the line of collision but also sideways. The gas that was in the middle of the groups moves both forward and sideways. Because it takes less time for the gas to reach balance in these directions, the temperature difference between ions and electrons is bigger in the directions that are at angles of plus or minus 45 degrees from the collision line. The electrons could be up to half as hot as the average temperature of the gas. Our findings might help explain what we see in X-ray images of these galaxy groups.

We examine the temporal dynamics of the intracluster medium during a merger event, with particular emphasis on the relaxation dynamics between ion and electron populations as modeled through N-body and hydrodynamical frameworks. Upon collision, subclusters generate a bow shock at their centers, which propagates symmetrically along the collisional axis. This shock mechanism primarily imparts thermal energy to ions, owing to the mass ratio disparity between ion and electron kinetic energies. In the downstream region, energy is subsequently transferred from ions to electrons through Coulombic coupling, though the complexity of this process escalates with variations in local gas density and temperature, particularly during the post-collisional expansion phase. Post-merger, gas dynamics exhibit bidirectional outflow, not merely along the collision axis but also in perpendicular directions. Initially central gas components are displaced both parallel and perpendicular to the axis, leading to a differential thermal equilibrium timescale across these directions. Consequently, the ion-electron temperature disparity intensifies in regions inclined at ±45° relative to the collision axis. The electron temperature may fall as much as 50% below the plasma mean temperature. These findings hold significant implications for the interpretation of X-ray observational data, offering a nuanced perspective on the thermodynamic structure of merging cluster environments.

We ride the turbulent wave of cosmic collision, where subclusters crash into each other like titanic ships in a storm, and the intracluster medium is tossed about like a sailor’s life raft. Between them, a bow shock forms—a crackling barrier that races out in both directions along the axis of impact, heating the ions like a forge, for their kinetic energy is far greater than that of the electrons, a difference as vast as the gap between a mountain and a molehill. In the wake of this shock, energy flows from ions to electrons, a slow dance of Coulomb coupling, but the timing of this exchange is as capricious as a drunken sailor, depending on the density and temperature of the gas. The electron temperature, once thought to follow the plasma mean temperature like a shadow, now wavers in complexity, especially as the gas expands and the dance of particles grows more tangled. After the crash, gas doesn’t just flee down the collision axis—it spirals outward in all directions, a chaotic swirl of particles once confined to the core. The equilibrium of this gas is swift, and so the temperature difference between ions and electrons grows most pronounced in the directions tilted at ±45 degrees from the axis. In these angles, the electron temperature might dip as low as half the plasma mean temperature, a stark contrast to the calm of the average. Our findings, a storm in the quiet of X-ray observations, hint at the hidden drama of the universe’s most violent collisions.

We investigate multi-spacecraft observations of the January 17, 2010 solar energetic particle event. Energetic electrons and protons have been observed over a remarkable large longitudinal range at the two STEREO spacecraft and SOHO suggesting a longitudinal spread of nearly 360 degrees at 1AU. The flaring active region, which was on the backside of the Sun as seen from Earth, was separated by more than 100 degrees in longitude from the magnetic footpoints of each of the three spacecraft. The event is characterized by strongly delayed energetic particle onsets with respect to the flare and only small or no anisotropies in the intensity measurements at all three locations. The presence of a coronal shock is evidenced by the observation of a type II radio burst from the Earth and STEREO B. In order to describe the observations in terms of particle transport in the interplanetary medium, including perpendicular diffusion, a 1D model describing the propagation along a magnetic field line (model 1) (Dr\"oge, 2003) and the 3D propagation model (model 2) by (Dr\"oge et al., 2010) including perpendicular diffusion in the interplanetary medium have been applied, respectively. While both models are capable of reproducing the observations, model 1 requires injection functions at the Sun of several hours. Model 2, which includes lateral transport in the solar wind, reveals high values for the ratio of perpendicular to parallel diffusion. Because we do not find evidence for unusual long injection functions at the Sun we favor a scenario with strong perpendicular transport in the interplanetary medium as explanation for the observations.

We looked at data from several spacecraft during a solar particle event on January 17, 2010. Energetic electrons and protons were seen over a very wide range of directions by two spacecraft and SOHO, showing that particles spread nearly all the way around the Sun at 1 AU. The solar flare was on the far side of the Sun from Earth, more than 100 degrees away from where the three spacecraft were looking. The event had a big delay between the flare and when the particles arrived. There wasn't much difference in how strong the particles were measured at the three places. A type II radio burst was heard from Earth and one of the STEREO spacecraft, showing a coronal shock. To explain the data, we used two models. One model showed how particles move along magnetic lines (model 1) and another showed 3D movement including sideways spread (model 2). Both models fit the data, but model 1 needed particles to be injected from the Sun over several hours. Model 2, which includes sideways movement in the solar wind, showed a high ratio of sideways to straight movement. Since we didn't find long injection times at the Sun, we think the main reason for the wide spread is strong sideways movement in space.

We examine the multi-spacecraft data from the January 17, 2010 solar energetic particle event, revealing a striking longitudinal extent in the distribution of energetic electrons and protons detected by the STEREO spacecraft and SOHO. This suggests a near-360-degree longitudinal spread at 1 AU, with the flaring active region, located on the Sun's backside as viewed from Earth, positioned over 100 degrees away from the magnetic footpoints of each of the three spacecraft. The event exhibits delayed particle onsets relative to the flare, accompanied by minimal intensity anisotropies across all three observation points. A coronal shock is corroborated by the detection of a type II radio burst from Earth and STEREO B. To interpret these observations through the lens of particle transport in the interplanetary medium, including perpendicular diffusion, two models have been applied: a 1D model (model 1) describing propagation along a magnetic field line (Dr\"oge, 2003), and a 3D model (model 2) incorporating perpendicular diffusion (Dr\"oge et al., 2010). While both models reproduce the data, model 1 necessitates injection functions at the Sun spanning several hours. Model 2, which accounts for lateral transport in the solar wind, indicates elevated ratios of perpendicular to parallel diffusion. Given the absence of evidence for extended injection functions at the Sun, we advocate a scenario involving robust perpendicular transport in the interplanetary medium as the explanatory framework for these observations.

We tracked the January 17, 2010 solar energetic particle event through the eyes of two STEREO spacecraft and SOHO, revealing a stunning spread of electrons and protons across nearly 360 degrees of longitude at 1AU. The flaring active region, hidden behind the Sun from Earth's view, was more than 100 degrees away from the magnetic footpoints of each spacecraft. The event unfolded slowly—energetic particles arrived long after the flare, with minimal intensity differences across the three observation points. A coronal shock was confirmed by the type II radio bursts heard on Earth and STEREO B. To explain these strange observations, we turned to two models: model 1, a 1D path along a magnetic field line (Dr\"oge, 2003), and model 2, a 3D journey through the solar wind (Dr\"oge et al., 2010), both accounting for perpendicular diffusion. Both models fit the data, but model 1 needed long injection times at the Sun. Model 2, however, showed a high ratio of perpendicular to parallel diffusion, hinting at fierce lateral movement in the solar wind. Since we found no hint of unusual injection times, we lean toward a scenario where the interplanetary medium itself is the key, with strong perpendicular transport driving the strange spread of particles.

AIM: We have recently developed a microscopic Monte Carlo approach to study surface chemistry on interstellar grains and the morphology of ice mantles. The method is designed to eliminate the problems inherent in the rate-equation formalism to surface chemistry. Here we report the first use of this method in a chemical model of cold interstellar cloud cores that includes both gas-phase and surface chemistry. The surface chemical network consists of a small number of diffusive reactions that can produce molecular oxygen, water, carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, methanol and assorted radicals. METHOD: The simulation is started by running a gas-phase model including accretion onto grains but no surface chemistry or evaporation. The starting surface consists of either flat or rough olivine. We introduce the surface chemistry of the three species H, O and CO in an iterative manner using our stochastic technique. Under the conditions of the simulation, only atomic hydrogen can evaporate to a significant extent. Although it has little effect on other gas-phase species, the evaporation of atomic hydrogen changes its gas-phase abundance, which in turn changes the flux of atomic hydrogen onto grains. The effect on the surface chemistry is treated until convergence occurs. We neglect all non-thermal desorptive processes. RESULTS: We determine the mantle abundances of assorted molecules as a function of time through 2x10^5 yr. Our method also allows determination of the abundance of each molecule in specific monolayers. The mantle results can be compared with observations of water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methanol ices in the sources W33A and Elias 16. Other than a slight underproduction of mantle CO, our results are in very good agreement with observations.

Although it has minimal impact on other gas-phase species, the evaporation of atomic hydrogen alters its gas-phase abundance, which in turn modifies the flux of atomic hydrogen onto grains. The effect on surface chemistry is processed until convergence is achieved. Non-thermal desorptive processes are disregarded. RESULTS: Mantle abundances of various molecules are determined as a function of time over 2×10⁵ years. The method also enables the determination of the abundance of each molecule in specific monolayers. Mantle results can be compared with observations of water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methanol ices in the sources W33A and Elias 16. Except for a minor underproduction of mantle CO, the results are in excellent agreement with observations.

We've made a new way to study how chemicals act on tiny particles in space. This method helps avoid some problems with old ways of looking at surface chemistry. Now we're using it in a model of cold space clouds, where both gas and surface reactions happen. The surface has a few simple reactions that can make oxygen, water, carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, methanol, and other small particles. 

We start by running a gas model that includes particles sticking to grains, but no surface reactions. The grains are either flat or rough, like olivine. Then we add reactions for hydrogen, oxygen, and carbon monoxide step by step, using our random method. In the simulation, only hydrogen can leave the surface much. Even though it doesn't change other gas things much, it changes how much hydrogen is in the gas, which affects how much hits the grains. We keep checking until everything settles down. We don't include any fast or unusual ways particles leave the surface.

We track how much of each molecule is on the surface over 200,000 years. We can also see how much is in each layer. We compare our results with what's seen in space, like ice in W33A and Elias 16. Except for a little bit less carbon monoxide, our results match what's observed really well.

We have recently engineered a microscopic Monte Carlo framework to interrogate surface chemistry on interstellar grains and the morphological architecture of ice mantles, eschewing the limitations of rate-equation formalisms in this domain. Herein, we present the inaugural application of this method within a chemical model of cold interstellar cloud cores, integrating both gas-phase and surface chemical processes. The surface chemical network comprises a limited set of diffusive reactions capable of synthesizing molecular oxygen, water, carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, methanol, and various radicals. The simulation commences with a gas-phase model incorporating accretion onto grains, excluding surface chemistry or evaporation. The initial surface is either flat or rough olivine. Surface chemistry for the species H, O, and CO is introduced iteratively via our stochastic methodology. Under simulation conditions, only atomic hydrogen exhibits significant evaporation. While this process has minimal impact on other gas-phase species, its evaporation alters the gas-phase abundance of hydrogen, thereby modifying the flux of atomic hydrogen onto grains. This effect is iteratively modeled until convergence is achieved, with non-thermal desorptive processes entirely disregarded. We ascertain the mantle abundances of various molecules as a function of time over 2×10⁵ years. Our method further enables the determination of molecular abundances within specific monolayers. Mantle results can be juxtaposed with observational data on water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methanol ices in the sources W33A and Elias 16. Except for a minor underproduction of mantle CO, our findings align closely with observations.

We've crafted a microscopic Monte Carlo approach to probe the chemistry of interstellar grains and the shape of their icy coatings—avoiding the pitfalls of traditional rate-equation methods. Here's how we've applied it: in a model of cold cloud cores, we've woven both gas-phase and surface reactions into a single tapestry. The surface chemistry is a tight-knit network of diffusive steps, capable of weaving oxygen, water, carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, methanol, and a host of radicals into existence. 

We begin with a gas-phase model, where grains accrete but surface reactions are held at bay. The grains start as flat or rough olivine, their surfaces waiting to be touched. Then, we introduce the chemistry of hydrogen, oxygen, and carbon monoxide, one step at a time, through our stochastic lens. Under these conditions, only atomic hydrogen can escape, a subtle but vital thread in the fabric of the gas. Though it affects few other species, its evaporation alters its own abundance, shifting the flow of hydrogen onto the grains. This dance continues until the numbers settle, until the system finds its rhythm.

Over 200,000 years, we track the abundance of molecules in the mantle, slicing through layers to find their concentrations. We compare these results with the ices observed in W33A and Elias 16—water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methanol. Except for a slight shortage of CO in the mantle, our findings align closely with what's seen in the cosmos.

The next generation of cosmology space missions will be sensitive to parasitic signals arising from cosmic rays. Using a composite bolometer, we have investigated pulses produced by $\alpha$ particles in order to understand the movement of energy produced by ionising radiation. Using a series of measurements at 100 mK, we have compared the typical fitting algorithm (a mathematical model) with a second method of pulse interpretation by convolving the detector's thermal response function with a starting profile of thermalised athermal phonons, taking into account the effects of heat propagation. Using this new fitting method, we have eliminated the need for a non-physical quadratic nonlinearity factor produced using more common methods, and we find a pulse form in good agreement with known aspects of thermal physics. This work is carried forward in the effort to produce a physical model for energy deposition in this detector. The modelling is motivated by the reproduction of statistical features in the experimental dataset, and the new interpretation of $\alpha$ pulse shapes represents an improvement in the current understanding of the energy propagation mechanisms in this detector.

The cosmos is about to unveil its secrets with a new wave of space missions, keen to catch the whispers of cosmic rays in their wake. We’ve built a composite bolometer to listen for the whispers of alpha particles, trying to trace the energy they leave in their wake. At 100 mK, we’ve tested two ways of reading these pulses: one a mathematical model, the other a more nuanced approach, blending the detector’s thermal response with a starting shape of thermalized athermal phonons, all while watching the heat move like a shadow. This new method cut through the noise, ditching a fake quadratic nonlinearity that had been bugging us before. The pulses we found fit nicely with what we know about heat, a sign that we’re getting closer to the truth. This work is part of a bigger push to build a real model of how energy settles in this detector. The model is driven by the need to match the stats in our data, and the new way we see alpha pulses is a step forward in understanding how energy moves through this detector like a current in a wire.

The next epoch in cosmological observation demands an acute sensitivity to parasitic signals generated by cosmic rays. Through the deployment of a composite bolometer, we have probed the temporal signatures of $\alpha$-particle interactions, aiming to elucidate the dynamics of energy release from ionising radiation. At temperatures of 100 mK, a sequence of measurements has juxtaposed a conventional mathematical model against an alternative approach: the convolution of the detector's thermal response function with an initial profile of athermal phonons, incorporating the diffusion of heat through the material. This novel methodology obviates the necessity for a non-physical quadratic nonlinearity term, typically introduced in conventional techniques, and yields a pulse morphology consistent with established principles of thermal dynamics. This research constitutes a critical step toward constructing a physical framework for energy deposition within the detector. The model is driven by the replication of statistical attributes in the experimental data, and the reinterpretation of $\alpha$-pulse shapes marks a significant advancement in the comprehension of energy transport mechanisms in this system.

The cosmos is about to unveil its secrets with a new wave of space missions, keen to catch the whispers of cosmic rays in their wake. We’ve built a composite bolometer to listen for the whispers of alpha particles, trying to trace the energy they leave in their wake. At 100 mK, we’ve tested two ways of reading these pulses: one a mathematical model, the other a more nuanced approach, blending the detector’s thermal response with a starting shape of thermalized athermal phonons, all while watching the heat move like a shadow. This new method cut through the noise, ditching a fake quadratic nonlinearity that had been bugging us before. The pulses we found fit nicely with what we know about heat, a sign that we’re getting closer to the truth. This work is part of a bigger push to build a real model of how energy settles in this detector. The model is driven by the need to match the stats in our data, and the new way we see alpha pulses is a step forward in understanding how energy moves through this detector like a current in a wire.

We consider an index data structure for similar strings. The generalized suffix tree can be a solution for this. The generalized suffix tree of two strings $A$ and $B$ is a compacted trie representing all suffixes in $A$ and $B$. It has $|A|+|B|$ leaves and can be constructed in $O(|A|+|B|)$ time. However, if the two strings are similar, the generalized suffix tree is not efficient because it does not exploit the similarity which is usually represented as an alignment of $A$ and $B$. In this paper we propose a space/time-efficient suffix tree of alignment which wisely exploits the similarity in an alignment. Our suffix tree for an alignment of $A$ and $B$ has $|A| + l_d + l_1$ leaves where $l_d$ is the sum of the lengths of all parts of $B$ different from $A$ and $l_1$ is the sum of the lengths of some common parts of $A$ and $B$. We did not compromise the pattern search to reduce the space. Our suffix tree can be searched for a pattern $P$ in $O(|P|+occ)$ time where $occ$ is the number of occurrences of $P$ in $A$ and $B$. We also present an efficient algorithm to construct the suffix tree of alignment. When the suffix tree is constructed from scratch, the algorithm requires $O(|A| + l_d + l_1 + l_2)$ time where $l_2$ is the sum of the lengths of other common substrings of $A$ and $B$. When the suffix tree of $A$ is already given, it requires $O(l_d + l_1 + l_2)$ time.

We're looking at a way to organize data for similar strings. A generalized suffix tree might work. This tree shows all the endings of two strings, A and B. It has as many leaves as the total length of the strings and can be built quickly. But if the strings are similar, this tree isn't very good. It doesn't use the similarity, which is usually shown by lining up A and B. 

In this paper, we suggest a better way. Our new suffix tree uses the alignment between A and B. It has more leaves than the old one, but in a smarter way. The number of leaves is the length of A plus some parts of B that are different and some parts that are the same. We didn't make the tree smaller by ignoring important parts. 

We can find a pattern in this tree quickly. It takes time equal to the pattern's length plus how many times it appears in A and B. We also have a fast way to build the tree. If we start from scratch, it takes time equal to the total length of the strings plus some extra parts. If we already have the tree for A, it's faster—just the extra parts.

We present a novel index structure for similar strings, wherein the generalized suffix tree proves insufficient due to its failure to leverage the inherent similarity between strings, typically encoded in their alignment. Our proposed structure, a suffix tree of alignment, optimally harnesses this similarity through a refined topological representation. For an alignment of strings $A$ and $B$, the tree possesses $|A| + l_d + l_1$ leaves, where $l_d$ denotes the aggregate length of divergent segments in $B$ relative to $A$, and $l_1$ signifies the cumulative length of shared subsequences. The design preserves the full capacity for pattern search, ensuring that no spatial efficiency is sacrificed in favor of functional completeness. A pattern $P$ may be located within the structure in $O(|P| + occ)$ time, with $occ$ representing the count of $P$’s occurrences across $A$ and $B$. The construction algorithm is both time and space efficient, requiring $O(|A| + l_d + l_1 + l_2)$ time when initiated from scratch, where $l_2$ is the sum of lengths of additional overlapping substrings. When leveraging an existing suffix tree for $A$, the construction time reduces to $O(l_d + l_1 + l_2)$. This framework thus achieves a harmonious balance between computational and spatial efficiency, aligning with the structural congruence of the underlying alignment.

We’re talkin’ about a data structure that can handle similar strings, and we’re lookin’ at the generalized suffix tree as a possible answer. This tree can hold all the suffixes of two strings, A and B, and it’s built to be compact, with leaves equal to the sum of the lengths of A and B. It’s constructed in linear time, which is pretty slick. But here’s the catch—if A and B are similar, this tree doesn’t cut it. It doesn’t take advantage of that similarity, which is usually shown as an alignment between the two. So we’re proposin’ a new suffix tree that’s built around that alignment, smartly usin’ the similarity to save space and time. Our tree has leaves equal to the sum of A’s length, plus the parts of B that differ from A, plus some common parts of A and B. We didn’t skimp on the pattern search to save space. This tree can find a pattern P in time proportional to the length of P plus the number of times it shows up in A and B. We also have an efficient way to build this tree. If we start from scratch, it takes time proportional to the sum of A’s length, the differing parts of B, and the common substrings. But if we already have A’s tree, it’s just the differing parts, the common parts, and the other common substrings. Clean, efficient, and built for similarity.

Materials with coupled or competing order parameters display highly tunable ground states, where subtle perturbations reveal distinct electronic and magnetic phases. These phases generally are underpinned by complex crystal structures, but the role of structural complexity in these phases often is unclear. We use group theoretic methods and first-principles calculations to analyze a set of coupled structural distortions that underlie the polar charge- and orbitally- ordered antiferromagnetic ground state of $A$-site ordered SmBaMn$_2$O$_6$. We show that these distortions play a key role in establishing the ground state and stabilizing a network of domain wall vortices. Furthermore, we show that the crystal structure provides a knob to control competing electronic and magnetic phases at structural domain walls and in epitaxially strained thin films. These results provide new understanding of the complex physics realized across multiple length scales in SmBaMn$_2$O$_6$ and demonstrate a framework for systematic exploration of correlated and structurally complex materials.

We apply group theoretical methods and first-principles calculations to examine a set of coupled structural distortions underlying the polar charge- and orbitally ordered antiferromagnetic ground state of A-site ordered SmBaMn$_2$O$_6$. We demonstrate that these distortions are essential for defining the ground state and stabilizing a network of domain wall vortices. Additionally, we show that the crystal structure serves as a means to control competing electronic and magnetic phases at structural domain walls and in epitaxially strained thin films. These findings offer new insights into the complex physics across multiple length scales in SmBaMn$_2$O$_6$ and establish a framework for systematic investigation of correlated and structurally complex materials.

Materials with linked or fighting order parts have special, adjustable base states. Small changes can show different electronic and magnetic states. These states often come from complicated crystal shapes, but it's not clear how the shape affects the states. We used math and computer models to look at some linked crystal changes that help make the base state of SmBaMn₂O₆. We found these changes help set the base state and keep a pattern of tiny loops. Also, the crystal shape helps control different electronic and magnetic states at these loops and in thin films. Our results help explain the tricky physics in SmBaMn₂O₆ and show a way to study linked and complex materials.

These configurations are typically supported by intricate crystal lattices, yet the contribution of structural intricacy remains ambiguously defined. We demonstrate that these deformations are pivotal in defining the ground state and in stabilizing a lattice of domain wall vortices. Moreover, we show that the crystal lattice functions as a regulatory mechanism for managing competing electronic and magnetic states at domain wall interfaces and within epitaxially strained thin films. These findings offer a novel comprehension of the multifaceted physics spanning multiple length scales in SmBaMn$_2$O$_6$, and establish a systematic approach for exploring correlated and structurally complex materials.

Water drop impacting a superhydrophobic surface (SHS) rebounds completely with remarkable elasticity. For such an impact, the balance between the inertial and capillary forces ascertain the contact time. This is found to be fairly constant for any macroscopically flat SHS and for a given drop volume. Recently, various studies have shown that breaking the radial symmetry during the drop impact can significantly reduce the contact time below that of a flat SHS. One such study has been performed on a cylindrical SHS with a curvature comparable to the drop. The reduction in contact time has been attributed to the radially anisotropic flow imparted by the tangential component of momentum and the elliptical footprint of the drop during the crash. Here, we perform drop impact experiments on bathtub-like SHS and show that the radial anisotropy can be triggered even in the absence of both the criteria mentioned above. This is shown to be a consequence of the lamella deflection during the spreading of the drop. The reduction in contact time is quite clearly evident in this experimental regime.

A water drop hits a superhydrophobic surface and bounces right back up, almost like it never touched the surface. When a drop hits, two forces — one from the drop moving and one from surface tension — work together to decide how long the drop stays in contact. This time is about the same for any flat SHS and for a drop of the same size. But new research shows that if you make the drop hit in a way that's not round, like a cylinder, the drop leaves faster. This happens because the drop spreads out more and the water moves in different directions. Now, we tested a bathtub-shaped SHS and found that even without the usual reasons, the drop still leaves faster. This is because the water pushes up and down as it spreads. The drop leaves the surface quicker in this setup.

The rebound of a water droplet upon a superhydrophobic surface exhibits an extraordinary degree of elastic restitution, governed by the equilibrium of inertial and capillary forces that dictate the duration of contact. This contact time remains relatively invariant across macroscopically flat SHS and for a fixed drop volume. Recent investigations reveal that disrupting radial symmetry during impact can markedly shorten contact time relative to flat surfaces. A prior study on a cylindrical SHS, whose curvature matches the drop's, demonstrated this effect, attributing it to radially anisotropic flow driven by tangential momentum and the drop's elliptical footprint. Here, we conduct impact experiments on bathtub-like SHS, demonstrating that radial anisotropy can be induced independently of the previously identified criteria. This phenomenon is elucidated as a result of lamella deformation during drop spreading. The reduction in contact time is distinctly observable in this experimental configuration, underscoring the nuanced interplay between surface morphology and dynamic fluid behavior.

A water droplet slams into a superhydrophobic surface and bounces back with a springy vigor that defies gravity. The dance between inertia and surface tension sets the tempo of the collision, and for a flat SHS, this rhythm stays steady—no matter the drop’s size. But recent experiments have flipped the script: by breaking the drop’s symmetry, researchers have slashed the contact time, making the rebound faster than on a flat surface. One study used a cylinder shaped like a drinking glass, its curves matching the droplet’s size. The drop’s oval shape, plus the way liquid flows in a spiral, shortened the touch. Now, here’s the twist: we’ve tested a tub-like SHS and found that asymmetry can emerge without needing that cylinder or the oval footprint. It’s the droplet’s own bending—its lamella flaring out—as the key. The contact time shrinks, clearly, in this new setup. The droplet’s leap is no longer just a bounce—it’s a rebellion against the rules.

For probabilistic programs, it is usually not possible to automatically derive exact information about their properties, such as the distribution of states at a given program point. Instead, one can attempt to derive approximations, such as upper bounds on tail probabilities. Such bounds can be obtained via concentration inequalities, which rely on the moments of a distribution, such as the expectation (the first raw moment) or the variance (the second central moment). Tail bounds obtained using central moments are often tighter than the ones obtained using raw moments, but automatically analyzing central moments is more challenging. This paper presents an analysis for probabilistic programs that automatically derives symbolic upper and lower bounds on variances, as well as higher central moments, of cost accumulators. To overcome the challenges of higher-moment analysis, it generalizes analyses for expectations with an algebraic abstraction that simultaneously analyzes different moments, utilizing relations between them. A key innovation is the notion of moment-polymorphic recursion, and a practical derivation system that handles recursive functions. The analysis has been implemented using a template-based technique that reduces the inference of polynomial bounds to linear programming. Experiments with our prototype central-moment analyzer show that, despite the analyzer's upper/lower bounds on various quantities, it obtains tighter tail bounds than an existing system that uses only raw moments, such as expectations.

For probabilistic programs, it's hard to exactly figure out things like how states are spread out at certain points in the code. Instead, people try to get good enough guesses, like saying how likely it is for something to be far from the average. These guesses can be made using math rules that look at how a group of numbers behaves, like how big they are on average or how much they vary. Using these rules, people can make guesses about how unlikely it is for things to be way off. Guesses made with these rules are often better than others, but figuring them out is trickier. This paper talks about a way to automatically find good guesses for how spread out numbers are and other things that show how numbers vary. To make this work, they use a special math tool that looks at different ways numbers can change together. A big idea is using a new kind of recursion that works with different math rules at the same time. They also made a simple way to check these rules that works with repeated steps. They built this into a tool that uses a template to make guessing easier by turning it into a problem that can be solved with simple math. Tests show that even though their tool gives ranges for different things, it makes better guesses about how unlikely things are to be far off than a tool that only looks at averages.

O masters, lords, and rulers in all lands, Is this the handiwork you give to God, This monstrous thing distorted and soul-quenched? How will you ever straighten up this shape-; Touch it again with immortality; Give back the upward looking and the light; Rebuild in it the music and the dream; Make right the immemorial infamies, Perfidious wrongs, immedicable woes? O masters, lords, and rulers in all lands, How will the future reckon with this man? How answer his brute question in that hour When whirlwinds of rebellion shake the world? How shall you again touch it with immortality? How shall you return the upward gaze and the light? How shall you rebuild in it the music and the dream? How shall you right the ancient scandals, the treacherous wrongs, the inevitable woes?

O masters, lords, and rulers throughout the world, how will the future judge this man? How shall you answer his brutal question in that moment when whirlwinds of rebellion shake the world? How shall it be with kingdoms and with kings—those who shaped him into what he is—when this silent terror shall reply to God after the silence of the centuries?

Edwin Markham

I. At the eleventh hour, the story begins. II. At war with society, the characters face challenges. III. A friendly chat happens between characters. IV. The house on Clapham Common is a key location. V. The inner circle consists of close friends. VI. New friends are introduced. VII. The daughter of Natas is a significant character. VIII. Learning the part involves preparation. IX. The beginning of sorrows occurs. X. The "Ariel" is a important object. XI. First blood is shed. XII. In the master's name, actions are taken. XIII. For life or death, decisions are made. XIV. The psychological moment is a turning point. XV. A voyage of discovery takes place. XVI. A wooing in mid-air happens. XVII. Aeria Felix is a name or place. XVIII. A navy of the future is imagined. XIX. The eve of battle is approaching. XX. Between two lives, choices are made. XXI. Just in time, events happen. XXII. Armed neutrality is a strategy. XXIII. A battle in the night occurs. XXIV. But the real historic strength of England, physical and moral, has never had anything to do with this athletic specialism; it has been rather hindered by it. Somebody said that the Battle of Waterloo was won on Eton playing-fields. It was a particularly unfortunate remark, for the English contribution to the victory of Waterloo depended very much more than is common in victories upon the steadiness of the rank and file in an almost desperate situation. The Battle of Waterloo was won by the stubbornness of the common soldier—that is to say, it was won by the man who had never been to Eton. It was absurd to say that Waterloo was won on Eton cricket-fields. But it might have been fairly said that Waterloo was won on the village green, where clumsy boys played a very clumsy cricket. In a word, it was the average of the nation that was strong, and athletic glories do not indicate much about the average of a nation. Waterloo was not won by good cricket-players. But Waterloo was won by bad cricket-players, by a mass of men who had some minimum of athletic instincts and habits. It is a good sign in a nation when such things are done badly. It shows that all the people are doing them. And it is a bad sign in a nation when such things are done very well, for it shows that only a few experts and eccentrics are doing them, and that the nation is merely looking on. Suppose that whenever we heard of walking in England it always meant walking forty-five miles a day without fatigue. We should be perfectly certain that only a few men were walking at all, and that all the other British subjects were being wheeled about in Bath-chairs. But if when we hear of walking it means slow walking, painful walking, and frequent fatigue, then we know that the mass of the nation still is walking. We know that England is still literally on its feet.
