But the real muscle and mettle of England, both body and soul, have never been about that one sport; they’ve been held back by it. Someone once claimed Waterloo was won on Eton’s turf. A cruel joke, for the real English punch in that battle came not from the elite, but from the ordinary soldier—men who’d never set foot in a cricket club. It was the grit of the common man, the guy who’d never played a game of cricket, that turned the tide. To say Waterloo was won on Eton fields was like saying a symphony was composed by a single note. Yet it might have been true to say Waterloo was won on a village green, where boys with clumsy sticks tried to hit a ball that didn’t want to be hit. In short, it was the average of the nation that made England strong, and the glory of the athlete tells us little about the average. Waterloo wasn’t won by the best cricketers, but by the worst—by a crowd of men with just enough athleticism to get the job done. It’s a good sign when a nation does things badly. It means the whole thing is in motion. But it’s a bad sign when a nation does things well, for that means only a few are in motion, and the rest are just spectators. Imagine if every time we heard of walking in England, it meant walking forty-five miles a day without a single drop of sweat. We’d know only a few men were walking, and the rest were just lying around in Bath chairs. But if walking in England means slow, painful, and frequently tired walking, then we know the nation is still on its feet. We know England is still standing.

The real strength of England, both physically and morally, has never come from being good at sports. In fact, it's often held back by that. Someone once said the Battle of Waterloo was won on Eton playing fields. That was a bad thing to say. The real reason England won Waterloo was because of the steady, tough work of the average soldier. Those soldiers hadn't gone to Eton. It didn't make sense to say Waterloo was won because of good cricket players. But it did make sense to say it was won by men who played bad cricket, men who were just average. The whole country's strength comes from the average person. Being good at sports doesn't show much about the average person. Waterloo was won by people who weren't really good at sports. But that's a good thing. It means everyone is doing it. If everyone was good at walking, that would mean only a few people were walking. But if everyone is just barely walking, that means the whole country is still moving. If we always thought of walking as something people do for forty-five miles a day, we'd know only a few people walk. But if walking is just slow, painful, and tiring, that means most people are still walking. That means England is still standing.

The true historical vigor of England, both corporeal and moral, has never been tethered to this singular athletic pursuit; rather, it has been obstructed by it. A remark once made—that the Battle of Waterloo was secured on Eton’s playing fields—was particularly misguided. The English role in Waterloo’s triumph hinged more on the resolute endurance of the common soldier in a near-apocalyptic scenario than on any elite athletic prowess. The Battle was won by the tenacity of the ordinary man, that is, by the individual who had never set foot at Eton. To assert that Waterloo was won on Eton cricket fields was absurd. Yet it might have been apt to say that Waterloo was won on the village green, where unskilled boys engaged in a clumsy game. In essence, it was the median of the nation that conferred strength, and athletic triumphs offer little insight into the median of a people. Waterloo was not won by virtuoso cricketers. Rather, it was won by subpar cricketers, by a multitude of men possessing only a minimal aptitude for athletic endeavors. A nation’s strength is signaled when such feats are executed poorly, for it reveals that the populace is engaged in them. Conversely, a nation’s weakness is indicated when such feats are performed flawlessly, for it signifies that only a few specialists and eccentric individuals are engaged in them, while the rest observe from the sidelines. Consider if every mention of walking in England implied a daily march of forty-five miles without fatigue. We would be certain that only a few men walked at all, and the rest of the British populace was confined to Bath chairs. Yet if walking is described as slow, arduous, and frequently fatiguing, we know that the majority still walks. We know that England remains literally on its feet.

But the real muscle and mettle of England, both body and soul, have never been about that one sport; they’ve been held back by it. Someone once claimed Waterloo was won on Eton’s turf. A cruel joke, for the real English punch in that battle came not from the elite, but from the ordinary soldier—men who’d never set foot in a cricket club. It was the grit of the common man, the guy who’d never played a game of cricket, that turned the tide. To say Waterloo was won on Eton fields was like saying a symphony was composed by a single note. Yet it might have been true to say Waterloo was won on a village green, where boys with clumsy sticks tried to hit a ball that didn’t want to be hit. In short, it was the average of the nation that made England strong, and the glory of the athlete tells us little about the average. Waterloo wasn’t won by the best cricketers, but by the worst—by a crowd of men with just enough athleticism to get the job done. It’s a good sign when a nation does things badly. It means the whole thing is in motion. But it’s a bad sign when a nation does things well, for that means only a few are in motion, and the rest are just spectators. Imagine if every time we heard of walking in England, it meant walking forty-five miles a day without a single drop of sweat. We’d know only a few men were walking, and the rest were just lying around in Bath chairs. But if walking in England means slow, painful, and frequently tired walking, then we know the nation is still on its feet. We know England is still standing.

Neither make too much of flaws and occasional overstatements. Some persons seem to think that absolute truth, in the form of rigidly stated propositions, is all that conversation admits. This is precisely as if a musician should insist on having nothing but perfect chords and simple melodies,—no diminished fifths, no flat sevenths, no flourishes, on any account. Now it is fair to say, that, just as music must have all these, so conversation must have its partial truths, its embellished truths, its exaggerated truths. It is in its higher forms an artistic product, and admits the ideal element as much as pictures or statues. One man who is a little too literal can spoil the talk of a whole tableful of men of *esprit*.—"Yes," you say, "but who wants to hear fanciful people's nonsense? Put the facts to it, and then see where it is!"—Certainly, if a man is too fond of paradox,—if he is flighty and empty,—if, instead of striking those fifths and sevenths, those harmonious discords, often so much better than the twinned octaves, in the music of thought,—if, instead of striking these, he jangles the chords, stick a fact into him like a stiletto. But remember that talking is one of the fine arts,—the noblest, the most important, and the most difficult,—and that its fluent harmonies may be spoiled by the intrusion of a single harsh note. Therefore conversation which is suggestive rather than argumentative, which lets out the most of each talker's results of thought, is commonly the pleasantest and the most profitable. It is not easy, at the best, for two persons talking together to make the most of each other's thoughts, there are so many of them.

This is akin to a musician insisting that a composition must consist solely of perfect chords and unadorned melodies—no diminished fifths, no flattened sevenths, no embellishments of any kind. Yet it is equally valid to assert that, just as music requires these variations, so too must conversation accommodate its partial truths, its embellished truths, its exaggerated truths. In its higher forms, discourse is an artistic endeavor, as much a realm of ideals as painting or sculpture. A single individual who is overly literal can undermine the vitality of a gathering of men of *esprit*. “Yes,” one might retort, “but who desires to hear the nonsense of fanciful minds? Present the facts, and then observe the result!” Indeed, if a person is too enamored with paradox, too flighty and empty, if instead of striking those harmonious discords—often superior to the twin octaves of conventional thought—he jangles the chords, inserting a fact like a stiletto, then the discourse is marred. Remember, however, that conversation is one of the fine arts—the noblest, the most vital, and the most challenging—and that its fluid harmonies may be disrupted by a single harsh note. Thus, discourse that is suggestive rather than argumentative, that liberally releases the results of each participant’s thought, is typically the most enjoyable and the most fruitful. It is not easy, even at its best, for two individuals engaged in conversation to fully realize each other’s thoughts, for there are so many of them.

Then there are the sentimentalists, who are the largest class and who make the easiest work of social questions. In the study of the individual organism we know that normal physiology presents the greatest difficulties and is the essential basis for a correct study of diseases and remedies. We also know that popular knowledge of physiology is meager in the extreme, while popular notions attach almost entirely to diseases and to remedies. The same is true of society. The study of the structure and functions of the organs of society is long and difficult, and we have, as yet, accomplished very little towards it. We can hope to accomplish much only by a long study of history and a careful examination of institutions. I venture to say that no study except the highest mathematics has ever yet made such demands on the human mind as are made by sociology. We cannot make an experiment in sociology because we cannot dispose of the time, that is, of the lives of a body of men and women. We have to carry in mind a great number of variables, to weigh their value, and to deduce their resultant, although for many of them we can find no unit of measurement or comparison, and although we have no notation to help us. I think that we shall have to adopt some of these methods of the other sciences sooner or later, but at present I see no means of advancing sociology save by the cultivation of a trained judgment through the careful study of sociological phenomena and sequences.

Sentimentalists constitute the largest group and approach social issues with the greatest ease. In examining the individual organism, normal physiology presents the most significant challenges and forms the fundamental basis for understanding diseases and treatments. Popular understanding of physiology is extremely limited, while common knowledge predominantly concerns diseases and treatments. This pattern applies similarly to society. The study of societal structures and functions is lengthy and complex, and progress in this area remains minimal. Significant advancement can be achieved only through extensive historical study and meticulous analysis of institutions. I believe no discipline, except the highest mathematics, has ever required the human mind to exert such demands as sociology does. Experiments in sociology are impractical because we cannot control the time, that is, the lives of a group of individuals. We must consider numerous variables, assess their significance, and deduce their combined effects, despite the lack of a standard unit of measurement or comparison for many of them, and the absence of a notation to aid in this process. I believe we will eventually adopt some of the methods from other sciences, but at present, I see no means of advancing sociology except through the development of a well-trained judgment through the careful study of sociological phenomena and sequences.

Sentimentalists, the largest and most accessible group, take the simplest path through the maze of social issues. In the study of the body, normal function is the hardest to grasp, the foundation upon which all disease and cure rest. Yet, the public knows little of this, focusing instead on ailments and treatments. The same pattern holds for society. The structure and function of its organs are complex and elusive, and we've barely scratched the surface. Progress can only come through deep historical study and meticulous examination of customs and systems. I dare say no field, save the highest math, has ever taxed the mind so profoundly as sociology. Only through this sharpened judgment can we hope to unlock the truths hidden within the tangled web of human society.

Sentimentalists are the biggest group and often handle social issues the easiest. When we look at a person's body, we find that understanding how it works is tough and important for knowing about sicknesses and treatments. Most people don't know much about how the body works, but they know a lot about illnesses and cures. The same is true for society. Learning how society works is hard and we haven't really made much progress. We can only hope to learn more by studying history and looking at how things are set up. I think no subject except math has ever required so much thinking. We can't do experiments in society because we can't control people's lives. We have to think about many things at once, figure out how they affect each other, and see what happens, even when we can't measure them or compare them. I believe we'll have to use some of the ways other sciences use sooner or later, but right now, the only way to get better at sociology is to study it carefully and learn to think deeply about how society works.

President Lincoln in a note to Mayor Ramsey once wrote: "The lady bearer of this note says she has two sons who want to work. Set them at it if possible. Wanting work is so rare a want that it should be encouraged." A college officer in my position at the opening of the college year would not be inclined to agree with Mr. Lincoln, for half the correspondence which comes to my desk during the summer months has to do with men who either want to work, or who say they do, in order that they may defray their college expenses. There are so many of them that their correspondence becomes almost depressing at times, for I realize the disappointments and the difficulties which very many of these boys will encounter after they reach college, and their unfitness to do any definite work well. "I have been out of high school three years," one young fellow writes, "and have not been able to save any money. I want, however, very much to go to college. Can you secure a place for me to work where I can earn my board and room and such extra money as I shall need for my other small expenses?" This man, who has given all his time to work for three years and who has done nothing more than live, expects easily to carry a college course which in itself requires most of a man's time to do justice to, and at the same time to earn his living on the side. I get many such letters from those who feel that earning one's living and going to college are in no way incompatible. So much has been written about the fellows who have started to college without a cent and who have later been valedictorians of their classes and ultimately President of the United States, or at least a member of his cabinet, that the average high school boy has little conception of what sacrifice and deprivation such a procedure involves; if he did understand he would nat so often undertake it, or he would do so after more careful deliberation.

As a result, the average high school student has little understanding of the sacrifices and privations involved in such a path. If he did comprehend the nature of this endeavor, he would not so frequently embark on it, or he would do so after more thorough consideration.

I know how hard it is for many of these boys after they get to college, and how unprepared some of them are for real work. One young man writes, "I've been out of high school for three years and haven't saved any money. I really want to go to college. But, although palæontology is a comparatively youthful scientific speciality, the mass of materials with which it has to deal is already prodigious. In the last fifty years the number of known fossil remains of invertebrated animals has been trebled or quadrupled. The work of interpretation of vertebrate fossils, the foundations of which were so solidly laid by Cuvier, was carried on, with wonderful vigour and success, by Agassiz in Switzerland, by Von Meyer in Germany, and last, but not least, by Owen in this country, while, in later years, a multitude of workers have laboured in the same field. In many groups of the animal kingdom the number of fossil forms already known is as great as that of the existing species. In some cases it is much greater; and there are entire orders of animals of the existence of which we should know nothing except for the evidence afforded by fossil remains. With all this it may be safely assumed that, at the present moment, we are not acquainted with a tithe of the fossils which will sooner or later be discovered. If we may judge by the profusion yielded within the last few years by the Tertiary formations of North America, there seems to be no limit to the multitude of Mammalian remains to be expected from that continent; and analogy leads us to expect similar riches in Eastern Asia, whenever the Tertiary formations of that region are as carefully explored. Again, we have as yet almost everything to learn respecting the terrestrial population of the Mesozoic epoch—and it seems as if the Western territories of the United States were about to prove as instructive in regard to this point as they have in respect of tertiary life. My friend Professor Marsh informs me that, within two years, remains of more than 160 distinct individuals of mammals, belonging to twenty species and nine genera, have been found in a space not larger than the floor of a good-sized room; while beds of the same age have yielded 300 reptiles, varying in size from a length of 60 feet or 80 feet to the dimensions of a rabbit.

Paleontology, though a relatively recent scientific discipline, confronts an archive of material so vast it defies measure. Within half a century, the catalog of known fossilized invertebrates has expanded threefold, or even fourfold, testifying to the relentless accumulation of evidence over time. The interpretation of vertebrate fossils, once anchored by Cuvier’s rigorous foundations, has since been propelled by the incisive scholarship of Agassiz, the meticulous analyses of Von Meyer, and the penetrating insights of Owen, with countless others contributing to the same endeavor. In numerous branches of the animal kingdom, the number of fossilized forms recognized now rivals or even surpasses the count of extant species. Entire taxonomic orders remain unknown to us save for the testimony of fossilized remains, underscoring the profound gap between what is observed and what is hidden. It is reasonable to posit that we have yet to grasp a single tenth of the fossilized remains that will inevitably emerge from the earth’s depths. Considering the Tertiary formations of North America, where the last few years have yielded an astonishing profusion of mammalian remains, one is compelled to infer that Eastern Asia, too, harbors an analogous trove, waiting only for the careful excavation of its stratified layers. The terrestrial inhabitants of the Mesozoic epoch remain largely uncharted, and the Western territories of the United States, already revealing their secrets in relation to Tertiary life, may yet offer comparable revelations regarding the ancient fauna that once thrived there. My friend Professor Marsh reports that within two years, more than 160 distinct mammalian remains, representing twenty species and nine genera, have been unearthed from an area no larger than the floor of a modest chamber, while strata of the same age have produced 300 reptiles, ranging in size from 60 to 80 feet to the diminutive proportions of a rabbit.

The interpretation of vertebrate fossils, once anchored by Cuvier’s rigorous foundations, has since been propelled by the incisive scholarship of Agassiz, the meticulous analyses of Von Meyer, and the penetrating insights of Owen, with countless others contributing to the same endeavor. In numerous branches of the animal kingdom, the number of fossilized forms recognized now rivals or even surpasses the count of extant species. Entire taxonomic orders remain unknown to us save for the testimony of fossilized remains, underscoring the profound gap between what is observed and what is hidden. It is reasonable to posit that we have yet to grasp a single tenth of the fossilized remains that will inevitably emerge from the earth’s depths. Considering the Tertiary formations of North America, where the last few years have yielded an astonishing profusion of mammalian remains, one is compelled to infer that Eastern Asia, too, harbors an analogous trove, waiting only for the careful excavation of its stratified layers. The terrestrial inhabitants of the Mesozoic epoch remain largely uncharted, and the Western territories of the United States, already revealing their secrets in relation to Tertiary life, may yet offer comparable revelations regarding the ancient fauna that once thrived there. My friend Professor Marsh reports that within two years, more than 160 distinct mammalian remains, representing twenty species and nine genera, have been unearthed from an area no larger than the floor of a modest chamber, while strata of the same age have produced 300 reptiles, ranging in size from 60 to 80 feet to the diminutive proportions of a rabbit.

Paleontology, though a young science, grapples with a treasure trove of fossils that stretch back through eons. In just fifty years, the number of known invertebrate fossils has multiplied by three or four. The study of vertebrates, once firmly rooted by Cuvier, has since been propelled by Agassiz, Von Meyer, and Owen, each adding fire and vigor to the field. Later, countless others have toiled in the same soil, uncovering the past with relentless determination. In many animal groups, the fossils we’ve found are as numerous as the living species today. In some cases, they’re more. There are entire orders of creatures whose existence we’d never know without the whispers of stone. Yet, we’ve only scratched the surface. The truth is, we know less than a tenth of what lies buried. If the Tertiary rocks of North America have yielded so much in recent years, what awaits in Eastern Asia when its layers are finally dug into? The Mesozoic, too, holds secrets yet untold, and the western U.S. seems poised to reveal as much as it has about the Tertiary. My friend Professor Marsh tells me that in two years, within the space of a room’s floor, over 160 mammal remains—twenty species, nine genera—have been uncovered. And in strata of the same age, 300 reptiles, from 60 to 80 feet long down to the size of a rabbit, have been found. The earth, in its silent patience, is still whispering its ancient stories.

Cross-examined.—I am an officer in the Grenadier Guards. I have had some experience of stage-plays. I believe that nothing is easier than to write a good stage-play. I have written one myself. I found it extremely easy. Mounting guard was an intellectual exercise not to be mentioned in the same breath with it. My play has not been produced—not yet. I have shown it to several managers—they hesitate to produce it, on the ground that it is too intellectual. I had no objection to bring it down to the comprehension of the audience; but I did not see any way of making it less intellectual than it was—I have no objection to state its name—it is a burlesque called *Tom Tiddler.*

Cross-examined.—I’m a grenadier, a man of steel and silence, yet I’ve danced on the edges of the stage, where words twist like rope around a man’s neck. I’ve always thought writing a play was as simple as breathing—light, easy, a matter of letting the words flow like a river through a mountain pass. I’ve done it. I’ve written one. And it was as simple as that. Guarding a post? That’s a mind-numbing chore, a task for a man with no soul. My play? It’s not yet on the boards. I’ve shown it to managers—men who fear the intellect, who shrink from the light. I didn’t mind lowering the bar, but I couldn’t make it less intellectual. I’ll say its name—*Tom Tiddler*, a burlesque, a joke dressed in the skin of tragedy.

Whatever was once the custom, in these days, at least, fraternity men are expected to pay their debts and to do so promptly. The young man with the buoyancy and optimism of Mr. Skimpole, in *[Bleak House](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Bleak_House),* who held that "the sordid word money should never be mentioned in the relations of friendship" is having little vogue at the present time. The enthusiastic life insurance agent, if you will admit his logic, can prove to you that if you will pay your premiums long enough they will cost you nothing, but every sensible man knows that the thing that is worth anything costs something, and the fraternity is no exception. Fraternity men in the past have too frequently taken their obligations lightly, and so in a financial way have brought fraternities into disrepute. Fraternity officers have begun strongly to emphasize the importance of financial matters in the fraternity and are insisting upon the introduction of accounting systems into all chapters which will make it possible for fraternity accounts to be kept accurately and which will impress upon the fraternity man from the outset his obligation to meet his bills when they are due. When a boy goes into a fraternity, neither he nor his father should be deceived as to the actual cost of membership, nor allowed to believe that payment may be evaded or deferred. It is ordinarily as unwise to go into a fraternity with the idea that the cost of living will thus be reduced as it is to enter matrimony with the thought that it will cost no more to support a family than an individual. With us at the University of Illinois the fraternity man is likely to be called upon to expend twenty per cent more than if he had remained outside of the organization, and if he develops popularity and contracts the joining habit, it may cost him considerably more than this.

Fraternity members are now expected to fulfill their financial obligations promptly. The youthful optimist, such as Mr. Skimpole from *Bleak House*, who believed that the term "money" should never be mentioned in friendships, is no longer widely admired. A dedicated life insurance salesman may argue that consistent premium payments eventually result in no cost, yet rational individuals recognize that value requires expenditure, and fraternities are no exception. Historically, fraternity members have often neglected their responsibilities, leading to financial reputational damage. To address this, fraternity leadership has intensified focus on financial accountability, implementing accounting systems in all chapters to ensure accurate record-keeping and to instill a sense of obligation to pay debts as they fall due. Upon joining a fraternity, neither the individual nor their father should be misled regarding the true cost of membership or allowed to believe payments can be postponed. It is as imprudent to join a fraternity expecting reduced living expenses as it is to marry with the notion that family support will cost no more than individual living. At the University of Illinois, fraternity members may find themselves spending twenty percent more than non-members, and if they gain popularity and develop a habit of joining, the cost could be significantly higher.

In the present era, the ethos of fraternities has shifted from a realm of lenient obligations to one of stringent fiscal accountability. The buoyant idealism of a character like Mr. Skimpole, whose creed dismissed the term "money" from the lexicon of camaraderie, has yielded to a more pragmatic approach. The enthusiastic salesperson of life insurance, if one is willing to concede the validity of his reasoning, may argue that prolonged adherence to premium payments will render them effectively gratis; yet, the discerning individual recognizes that value is never without cost, and the fraternity, too, is no exception. Historically, the neglect of financial responsibilities by fraternity members has sullied the institution’s reputation, prompting a reorientation of priorities. Fraternity leadership now champions fiscal integrity, implementing accounting systems that ensure transparency and instill in each member an early awareness of their duty to fulfill obligations upon their due. Entry into a fraternity must not be misconstrued as a means to circumvent financial burdens, any more than marriage is viewed as a path to familial ease without sacrifice. At the University of Illinois, membership often incurs a twenty-per cent additional expense compared to non-member life, and the cultivation of popularity may escalate this cost substantially. Thus, the fraternity, once a sanctuary of moral flexibility, now stands as a bastion of fiscal discipline, where the old ideals of leniency have been supplanted by a new, rigorous ethic of responsibility.

Upon joining a fraternity, neither the individual nor their father should be misled regarding the true cost of membership or allowed to believe payments can be postponed. It is as imprudent to join a fraternity expecting reduced living expenses as it is to marry with the notion that family support will cost no more than individual living. At the University of Illinois, fraternity members may find themselves spending twenty percent more than non-members, and if they gain popularity and develop a habit of joining, the cost could be significantly higher.

Fraternity men these days are expected to take their financial responsibilities seriously and pay them on time. The young man who once believed that talking about money in friendships was bad manners is not as popular now. A life insurance salesman might tell you that if you pay your premiums long enough, they'll cost you nothing, but most people know that things worth having usually cost something. Fraternities used to have members who didn't take their duties seriously, and that made the fraternities look bad. Now, fraternity leaders are pushing hard for financial responsibility. They want chapters to have proper books so they can keep track of money properly. They want each member to understand from the start that they must pay what they owe when it's due. When a boy joins a fraternity, neither he nor his father should think that joining will lower his costs or that payments can be put off. It's just as silly to join a fraternity thinking it will save money as it is to get married expecting it will cost no more than being alone. At the University of Illinois, a fraternity member might end up spending twenty percent more than someone who didn't join. If he becomes popular and starts attracting more members, the cost could be much higher.

In the present era, the ethos of fraternities has shifted from a realm of lenient obligations to one of stringent fiscal accountability. The buoyant idealism of a character like Mr. Skimpole, whose creed dismissed the term "money" from the lexicon of camaraderie, has yielded to a more pragmatic approach. The enthusiastic salesperson of life insurance, if one is willing to concede the validity of his reasoning, may argue that prolonged adherence to premium payments will render them effectively gratis; yet, the discerning individual recognizes that value is never without cost, and the fraternity, too, is no exception. Historically, the neglect of financial responsibilities by fraternity members has sullied the institution’s reputation, prompting a reorientation of priorities. Fraternity leadership now champions fiscal integrity, implementing accounting systems that ensure transparency and instill in each member an early awareness of their duty to fulfill obligations upon their due. Entry into a fraternity must not be misconstrued as a means to circumvent financial burdens, any more than marriage is viewed as a path to familial ease without sacrifice. At the University of Illinois, membership often incurs a twenty-per cent additional expense compared to non-member life, and the cultivation of popularity may escalate this cost substantially. Thus, the fraternity, once a sanctuary of moral flexibility, now stands as a bastion of fiscal discipline, where the old ideals of leniency have been supplanted by a new, rigorous ethic of responsibility.

Fraternity men these days are expected to honor their debts, and not just any debts—those of the brotherhood. The buoyant Mr. Skimpole, with his airy refusal to speak of money in the realm of friendship, is a relic of a bygone era. The insurance man, with his zeal, might argue that if you pay long enough, the cost vanishes, but sense tells us otherwise. What's worth having costs something, and fraternities are no exception. In the past, brothers too often treated their pledges lightly, and in doing so, brought disgrace to the name of the brotherhood. Now, the officers are making it clear: money matters. They're pushing for accounting systems that'll keep tabs on every penny, making it plain for all that dues are dues, and that no one gets off the hook. When a boy joins, neither he nor his father should be fooled into thinking the price is low or that payments can be delayed. It's as foolish to join a brotherhood expecting cheaper living as it is to marry expecting a free hand. At Illinois, the cost is real—twenty percent more than if he'd stayed outside. And if he gains popularity, the price may rise even higher, a toll for the privilege of being part of the brotherhood.

Merited and timely as such criticism may appear to a transient observer of the State university, it is recognized as superficial and essentially false by all those who have felt the inner throb and glow of the enterprise. Idealist the institution is not, if idealism means a sterile yearning for the unattainable. Materialist it is not, if materialism is identified with satisfaction in the welfare of the senses. The State university to-day is at the same time intensely visionary and intensely practical: its driving power is the creative artist's desire to externalize and eternize his dream. With eyes fixed upon that end, it does not shrink from the coarse tasks of mixing pigments, quarrying stone, or melting bronze. It would honor every truth by use, and it holds that the triumph of the spiritual is the subjugation of the material. The financial support which it solicits is the means to the realization of a vision embracing almost the whole of life, and the wealth which it helps to create is but the first fruits of its contemplated harvest.

The criticism of the State university, though justified to a passing observer, is acknowledged as superficial and inaccurate by those who have experienced the institution's inner vitality. The institution is not idealistic in the sense of aspiring to an unattainable utopia, nor is it materialistic in the sense of deriving pleasure from sensory indulgence. Contemporary State university is both visionary and practical; its core motivation is the artist's desire to manifest and immortalize his vision. Focused on this goal, it does not avoid the arduous tasks of mixing pigments, quarrying stone, or melting metal. It honors every truth through its application and holds that the victory of the spirit is the dominance of the material. The financial assistance it seeks is a means to achieve a vision encompassing nearly all aspects of life, and the wealth it generates is merely the initial yield of its intended achievements.

A State university, though seeming noble to a fleeting eye, pulses with a deeper, more vital truth. To those who have felt its soul, the criticism is not just shallow—it’s wrong. It’s not an idealist, not in the way that dreams of unreachable heavens are called idealism. Nor is it a materialist, not in the way that pleasure in the flesh is called materialism. Today’s university is both dreamer and doer, a place where the artist’s fire burns bright and the hands are ready to grind stone, mix colors, or melt metal. The enduring renown of our most distinguished comic dramatist rests entirely upon three of his five plays, the others contributing little to his legacy. His inaugural comedy, though a dazzling imitation of earlier works, is a fleeting echo of models eclipsed by his own early mastery; tragedy, in his hands, is rendered garish and frayed, as if smeared with the cosmetics of Lady Wishfort. Yet his three seminal comedies are sufficient to secure a reputation as enduring as our language itself. Without them, we would lack exemplars of comedy in its purest and most elevated form. [Ben Jonson](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Author:Ben_Jonson), the sole individual who endeavoured to introduce clarity into the muddled stagecraft of an age when comedy and tragedy were as entwined as the realities of life, failed to infuse his elaborate and magnificent work with the necessary lightness and grace of comic life and movement. Among Congreve’s immediate forebears, who sought to construct a new English comedy upon French foundations, Wycherley’s metal was too base and Etherege’s too flimsy to stand comparison; no finer currency than the coarse British ore of Shadwell’s brutal and robust talent was then in circulation. Borrowing a metaphor from [Landor](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Author:Walter_Savage_Landor), we may say that a single limb of Molière would have sufficed to make a Congreve, and a single limb of Congreve would have sufficed to make a [Sheridan](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Author:Richard_Brinsley_Sheridan). The robust and broad humour of [Vanbrugh’s](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Author:John_Vanbrugh) admirable comedies grants him a place among the masters.

Borrowing a metaphor from [Landor](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Author:Walter_Savage_Landor), we may say that a single limb of Molière would have sufficed to make a Congreve, and a single limb of Congreve would have sufficed to make a [Sheridan](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Author:Richard_Brinsley_Sheridan). The robust and broad humour of [Vanbrugh’s](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Author:John_Vanbrugh) admirable comedies grants him a place among the masters.

Ben Jonson's reputation as our greatest comic dramatist comes mostly from three of his five plays. His first comedy was just a smart copy of older plays, but it was so good that even the originals seemed less impressive by comparison. His tragedies look a bit fake, like they've been painted and powdered, much like Lady Wishfort. But his three big comedies are so good they've kept his name alive in our language. Without them, we wouldn't have any real examples of comedy at its best.

The only other writer around was Shadwell, but his work was rough and not very good.

The fame of our most esteemed comic dramatist is primarily based on three of his five plays. His first comedy was merely a brilliant imitation of earlier works, eclipsed by his own early effort. Tragedy, in his hands, appears exaggerated and affected, as seen in the character of Lady Wishfort. However, his three major comedies are sufficient to establish a reputation as enduring as our language. Without these, we would have no examples of comedy in its purest and highest form. Ben Jonson, who alone attempted to introduce a reform by separating comedy from tragedy during a period when the two genres were indistinguishably merged on the stage, failed to provide the necessary ease and grace of comic life and movement to his elaborate and magnificent work. We call it a singular fact, because we Yankees are thought to be fond of the spread-eagle style, and nothing can be more remote from that than his. We are reckoned a practical folks, who would rather hear about a new air-tight stove than about [Plato](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Author:Plato); yet our favorite teacher's practicality is not in the least of the Poor Richard variety. If he have any Buncombe constituency, it is that unrealized commonwealth of philosophers which Plotinus proposed to establish; and if he were to make an almanac, his directions to farmers would be something like this: "October: *Indian Summer;* now is the time to get in your early Vedas." What, then, is his secret? Is it not that he out-Yankees us all? that his range includes us all? that he is equally at home with the potato-disease and original sin, with pegging shoes and the Over-soul? that, as we try all trades, so has he tried all cultures? and above all, that his mysticism gives us a counterpoise to our super-practicality?

We term it a singular fact, for we Yankees are reputed to favor the spread-eagle posture, yet nothing is more alien to it than his. Regarded as a pragmatic people, inclined to favor the discourse of a new airtight stove over the musings of Plato, our favored teacher’s pragmatism is not of the Poor Richard sort. If he possesses any Buncombe following, it is the unrealized commonwealth of philosophers Plotinus envisioned. That, as we traverse all trades, so has he traversed all cultures? And above all, that his mysticism provides a counterbalance to our super-practicality.

If he possesses any Buncombe following, it is the unrealized commonwealth of philosophers Plotinus envisioned. Should he compose an almanac, his counsel to farmers might read: “October: *Indian Summer;* now is the time to harvest your early Vedas.” What, then, is his secret? Is it not that he out-Yankees us, that his domain encompasses us all, that he is equally at home with potato disease and original sin, with pegging shoes and the Over-soul? That, as we traverse all trades, so has he traversed all cultures? And above all, that his mysticism provides a counterbalance to our super-practicality.

The ancient proverb which declares that love is blind is only a half truth: love is only blind of one eye. The expression "blind hate" also contains only a half truth: hate has one powerful eye. When either of these passions is present, it insatiably sets about discovering new objects to feast upon. The lover collects and broods upon the graces of his beloved from the rising of the lark to the going down of the evening star. The husband who thoroughly loses his temper with his wife at the breakfast table busies himself all day long recollecting and amassing all the grievances that he has felt against her during the last ten years; and he returns at night in a sullen rage and with an almost superhuman insight into the deficiencies of his helpmate. So men of letters set out with gusto and find a relish in every wayside berry; or they set out on the satirical foot with a bad taste in their mouths, and for a whole generation occupy themselves with malicious caricatures of their mistress, Life.

The ancient proverb that love is blind reveals only one facet of its nature: love is blind in one eye, while the other remains keenly focused on the object of its desire. Similarly, the phrase "blind hate" is similarly incomplete: hate possesses a single, formidable eye that scans the world for vulnerabilities. When either of these passions manifests, it becomes an insatiable seeker, constantly expanding its domain in search of new prey. The lover, with one eye fixed on the beauty of his beloved, accumulates and ponders the virtues of his object from dawn to dusk. The husband, when enraged at his wife’s breakfast table, dedicates his entire day to cataloging and reflecting on the grievances he has harbored for a decade, returning at night with a tempestuous fury and an almost supernatural clarity of his spouse’s flaws. Thus, men of letters, too, embark with fervor, savoring every wild berry along the path, or launch with bitterness into the satire of their mistress, Life, occupying themselves for generations with the grotesque caricatures of their chosen target.

Love is blind in one eye, the ancient proverb says, but that's only half the story. Love fixes its gaze on one thing, while hate has a single, burning eye that scans the world for prey. When either passion stirs, it hungerously seeks new things to devour. The lover, from dawn till dusk, gathers the beauty of his beloved, each grace a jewel in his collection. The husband, when he loses his temper at breakfast, spends the day compiling grievances, a ledger of wounds, and returns at night with a fury that sees the world through the lens of his wife's flaws. So men of letters set out with fervor, savoring every wild berry along the way, or they launch their satire with a sour taste, spending a lifetime carving caricatures of their mistress, Life, with a knife that cuts deeper than any pen.

There was a still more pregnant reason for my desertion of the camp of musical criticism. I seemed always to be about ten years ahead of most of the other critics and the orchestral conductors who make out programs. I missed the reviling of Wagner in New York, but I have watched the pundits of the press revile, in turn, Richard Strauss, Debussy, and Stravinsky, only, in the end, after their ears, through repeated hearings, had grown accustomed to the new clang-tints, to accept these composers as part of the sacred hierarchy. My orchestral education was carried on under Theodore Thomas in Chicago. Now Thomas was not a great conductor, although he always gave honest musical readings of his scores, but he had one great virtue: he believed that new music should be heard. He performed, therefore, every important European composition as soon as possible after it had been performed abroad. As a result, when I arrived in New York in 1906, having listened to and appraised nearly all the major works of Strauss and Debussy composed up to that date, I was amazed to discover that the New York critics were still fighting about these composers, first underpraising them and a little later overpraising them, for Strauss, at any rate, to my mind, has never been a whit superior as a composer to such a man as Liszt. In Paris, in 1913, I heard Stravinsky's [Sacre du Printemps](https://en.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=Sacre_du_Printemps&action=edit&redlink=1) and a good deal more of this Russian's music. I wrote a panegyric about Le Sacre du Printemps in my first book,[[1]](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Red#cite_note-1) published in 1915. In 1924, Le Sacre du Printemps has at last been performed in New York and the critics have at last accepted Stravinsky. So, indeed, apparently, have the conductors who, until the past four years, hardly ever permitted his name to be emblazoned on their programs. The job of music critic in New York, therefore, is certainly not an ideal occupation for a man with imagination and foresight.

I left the camp of musical criticism for a reason that felt even more important. I always seemed to be about ten years ahead of the other critics and the conductors who put together programs. I missed the bad things people said about Wagner in New York, but I saw the critics there say bad things about Richard Strauss, Debussy, and Stravinsky. Eventually, after hearing these composers a lot, the critics got used to their music and started to accept them as part of the big group of composers. My music education was with Theodore Thomas in Chicago. Thomas wasn't a great conductor, though he always played the music honestly. But he had one good thing: he believed new music should be heard. He played every important European composition as soon as he could after it was played abroad. So when I got to New York in 1906, having heard and judged most of Strauss and Debussy's major works up to that time, I was surprised to find that New York critics were still arguing about these composers. They first said they weren't good and then said they were too good, especially for Strauss. But to me, Strauss wasn't much better than Liszt. In Paris in 1913, I heard Stravinsky's "The Rite of Spring" and a lot more of his music. I wrote a nice praise about it in my first book, published in 1915. In 1924, "The Rite of Spring" was finally played in New York and the critics accepted Stravinsky. So, it seems, did the conductors who hadn't even put his name on their programs in years. The job of being a music critic in New York isn't a good job for someone who has imagination and looks ahead.

I left the camp of musical criticism not just for the sake of a fleeting whim, but because I was always ten years ahead of the rest—those critics and conductors who clung to the old scores like a sailor to a leaky boat. I missed the jeers aimed at Wagner in New York, but I watched as the press pundits turned their ire upon Richard Strauss, Debussy, and Stravinsky, only to eventually accept them as part of the sacred pantheon, once their ears, after many hearings, had grown used to the new clang-tints. My orchestral education was under Theodore Thomas in Chicago. Thomas wasn’t a great conductor, though he always gave honest readings of the scores. But he had one great virtue: he believed in new music. He performed every important European composition as soon as it was played abroad. So when I arrived in New York in 1906, having listened to and judged nearly all of Strauss and Debussy’s major works up to that point, I was stunned to find the New York critics still squabbling over these composers—first underpraising, then overpraising, especially Strauss, whom I never found superior to Liszt. In Paris in 1913, I heard Stravinsky’s *Sacre du Printemps* and much more of this Russian’s music. I wrote a glowing tribute to it in my first book, published in 1915. By 1924, *Sacre du Printemps* had finally been performed in New York, and the critics had finally accepted Stravinsky. So, indeed, apparently, had the conductors who, until the past four years, had scarcely ever let his name appear on their programs. The job of a music critic in New York is surely not an ideal one for a man with imagination and foresight.

The abandonment of the camp of musical critique was not merely a retreat from convention but a reckoning with the temporal disjunction between perception and reception. I had long found myself a decade ahead of my peers, those critics and conductors who curated the repertory, their judgments shaped by a lag that rendered the new unfamiliar and the old immutable. The reviling of Wagner in New York had been a relic of a bygone era; yet the modern critics, in their ceaseless oscillation between underpraise and overpraise, had not yet transcended the same cycle, their ears, like the stubbornness of a child, refusing to adjust to the novel sonorities until they had been repeatedly and relentlessly exposed. My orchestral education, under Theodore Thomas, had been a crucible of progress. Though Thomas lacked the genius of a Maestros, his faith in the new music as a necessary and urgent phenomenon set him apart. He performed European works as soon as their foreign origins had been transcribed, thus granting me, upon my arrival in New York in 1906, a vantage point that left me bewildered by the critics’ continued squabbling over Strauss and Debussy. To me, Strauss was no more a master than Liszt, yet the critics, in their stubbornness, had not yet surrendered to this truth. In Paris, 1913, I encountered Stravinsky’s *Sacre du Printemps*, and in my first book, published in 1915, I extolled its genius. By 1924, the New York stage had at last embraced the work, and with it, the critics, who had long resisted its inclusion. Thus, the New York music critic’s vocation, in its present form, is not a calling for those who possess the vision to foresee the future of sound. It is a role bound by the inertia of tradition, a domain where the visionary is perpetually out of step.

The abandonment of the camp of musical critique was not merely a retreat from convention but a reckoning with the temporal disjunction between perception and reception. I had long found myself a decade ahead of my peers, those critics and conductors who curated the repertory, their judgments shaped by a lag that rendered the new unfamiliar and the old immutable. The reviling of Wagner in New York had been a relic of a bygone era; yet the modern critics, in their ceaseless oscillation between underpraise and overpraise, had not yet transcended the same cycle, their ears, like the stubbornness of a child, refusing to adjust to the novel sonorities until they had been repeatedly and relentlessly exposed. My orchestral education, under Theodore Thomas, had been a crucible of progress. Though Thomas lacked the genius of a Maestros, his faith in the new music as a necessary and urgent phenomenon set him apart. He performed European works as soon as their foreign origins had been transcribed, thus granting me, upon my arrival in New York in 1906, a vantage point that left me bewildered by the critics’ continued squabbling over Strauss and Debussy. To me, Strauss was no more a master than Liszt, yet the critics, in their stubbornness, had not yet surrendered to this truth. In Paris, 1913, I encountered Stravinsky’s *Sacre du Printemps*, and in my first book, published in 1915, I extolled its genius. By 1924, the New York stage had at last embraced the work, and with it, the critics, who had long resisted its inclusion. Thus, the New York music critic’s vocation, in its present form, is not a calling for those who possess the vision to foresee the future of sound. It is a role bound by the inertia of tradition, a domain where the visionary is perpetually out of step.

I left the camp of musical criticism not just for the sake of a fleeting whim, but because I was always ten years ahead of the rest—those critics and conductors who clung to the old scores like a sailor to a leaky boat. I missed the jeers aimed at Wagner in New York, but I watched as the press pundits turned their ire upon Richard Strauss, Debussy, and Stravinsky, only to eventually accept them as part of the sacred pantheon, once their ears, after many hearings, had grown used to the new clang-tints. My orchestral education was under Theodore Thomas in Chicago. Thomas wasn’t a great conductor, though he always gave honest readings of the scores. But he had one great virtue: he believed in new music. He performed every important European composition as soon as it was played abroad. So when I arrived in New York in 1906, having listened to and judged nearly all of Strauss and Debussy’s major works up to that point, I was stunned to find the New York critics still squabbling over these composers—first underpraising, then overpraising, especially Strauss, whom I never found superior to Liszt. In Paris in 1913, I heard Stravinsky’s *Sacre du Printemps* and much more of this Russian’s music. I wrote a glowing tribute to it in my first book, published in 1915. By 1924, *Sacre du Printemps* had finally been performed in New York, and the critics had finally accepted Stravinsky. So, indeed, apparently, had the conductors who, until the past four years, had scarcely ever let his name appear on their programs. The job of a music critic in New York is surely not an ideal one for a man with imagination and foresight.

First, there was a Teachers' Institute at the county-seat; and there distinguished guests of the superintendent taught the teachers fractions and spelling and other mysteries,—white teachers in the morning, Negroes at night. A picnic now and then, and a supper, and the rough world was softened by laughter and song. I remember how— But I wander. There came a day when all the teachers left the Institute and began the hunt for schools. I learn from hearsay (for my mother was mortally afraid of fire-arms) that the hunting of ducks and bears and men is wonderfully interesting, but I am sure that the man who has never hunted a country school has something to learn of the pleasures of the chase. I see now the white, hot roads lazily rise and fall and wind before me under the burning July sun; I feel the deep weariness of heart and limb as ten, eight, six miles stretch relentlessly ahead; I feel my heart sink heavily as I hear again and again, "Got a teacher? Yes." So I walked on and on—horses were too expensive—until I had wandered beyond railways, beyond stage lines, to a land of "varmints" and rattlesnakes, where the coming of a stranger was an event, and men lived and died in the shadow of one blue hill.

I glean from rumor (for my mother feared firearms) that the pursuit of ducks, bears, and men is profoundly engaging, though I am certain the man who has not hunted a country school lacks understanding of the pleasures of the chase. Now I see the white, scorching roads rise and fall, winding before me under the searing July sun; I feel the profound exhaustion of both heart and body as ten, eight, six miles stretch unrelentingly ahead; I feel my spirit sink as the call "Got a teacher? Yes." echoes again and again. Thus I walked on, on—horses too costly—until I had wandered beyond railways, beyond stage lines, to a land of "varmints" and rattlesnakes, where the arrival of a stranger was an event, and men lived and died in the shadow of one blue hill.

Sprinkled over hill and dale lay cabins and farmhouses, shut out from the world by the forests and the rolling hills toward the east. There I found at last a little school. Josie told me of it; she was a thin, homely girl of twenty, with a dark-brown face and thick, hard hair. I had crossed the stream at Watertown, and rested under the great willows; then I had gone to the little cabin in the lot where Josie was resting on her way to town. The gaunt farmer made me welcome, and Josie, hearing my errand, told me anxiously that they wanted a school over the hill; that but once since the war had a teacher been there; that she herself longed to learn,—and thus she ran on, talking fast and loud, with much earnestness and energy.

Cabins and farmhouses sat scattered across the hills and valleys, cut off from the world by forests and hills to the east. There I found a small school. Josie told me about it. She was a thin, plain girl twenty years old, with a dark face and thick, hard hair. I crossed the stream at Watertown, rested under the big willows, then went to the little cabin where Josie was staying on her way to town. The farmer was friendly and welcomed me. Josie, hearing why I came, said they needed a teacher up the hill. She said it had been years since someone taught there. She wanted to learn, and she talked quickly, loud, with real care and energy.

There is no agency like the home paper for developing a broad human interest and for keeping us in touch with the friendships and the ideals of our youth.

My bands of silk and miniver Momently grew heavier; The black gauze was beggarly thin; The ermine muffled mouth and chin; I could not suck the moonlight in. Harlequin in lozenges Of love and hate, I walked in these Striped and ragged rigmaroles; Along the pavement my footsoles Trod warily on living coals. Shouldering the thoughts I loathed, In their corrupt disguises clothed, Morality I could not tear From my ribs, to leave them bare Ivory in silver air. There I walked, and there I raged; The spiritual savage caged Within my skeleton, raged afresh To feel, behind a carnal mesh, The clean bones crying in the flesh.

My silk and miniver bands grew heavier, a weight of moments; the black gauze was pitifully thin, a beggar's shroud. The ermine muffled my mouth and chin, blocking the moonlight I longed to sip. A harlequin in lozenges of love and hate, I walked through striped, ragged rigmaroles. My footsoles tread warily on living coals, each step a warning. Shouldering thoughts I loathed, cloaked in corrupt disguises, morality clung to my ribs, a silver ivy in ivory air. There I walked, there I raged— the spiritual savage caged in my skeleton, roaring anew to feel the clean bones cry through the flesh.

Shouldering thoughts I despised, cloaked in corrupt disguises, morality could not be torn from my ribs to leave them bare ivory in silver air. There I walked, there I raged; the spiritual savage caged within my skeleton raged again to feel, behind a carnal mesh, the clean bones crying in the flesh.

Shall I compare thee to a summers day? Thou art more lovely and more temperate: Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May, And summers lease hath all too short a date; Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines, And often is his gold complexion dimm'd; And every fair from fair sometime declines, By chance or natures changing course untrimm'd; But thy eternal summer shall not fade, Nor lose possession of that fair thou owst; Nor shall death brag thou wanderst in his shade, When in eternal lines to time thou growst: So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.

Shall I compare thee to a summer's day? Thou art more lovely, more tempered than that fleeting bloom. Rough winds shake the tender buds of May, and summer's lease is too brief. The heavens' eye too often blazes hot, then dims to gold's dull hue. All beauty, fair or foul, must fade, by chance or nature's unerring turn. Yet thy eternal summer shall not wane, nor lose the fair thou dost possess. Death shall not claim thee, nor claim the light thou art. For in eternal lines, thou shalt grow, ever young, ever bright. So long as breath and eyes endure, so long this verse, and through it, thou shalt live.

Thou art more resplendent, more serene: tempests bruise thy tender bloom, and summer’s lease is but a fleeting breath; the heavens’ eye, too fervent, often dims its golden sheen; all beauty, fair or foul, must wane, by chance or by nature’s unerring course; yet thy eternal summer shall not fade, nor relinquish the fair thou becomest; nor shall death claim thee for its domain, when in eternal verse thou dost ascend: so long as breath and sight endure, so long shall this endure, and this, in turn, shall vivify thee.

Stella is sick, and in that sick-bed lies Sweetness, that breathes and pants as oft as she; And grace, sick too, such fine conclusions tries That sickness brags itself best graced to be. Beauty is sick, but sick in so fair guise That in that paleness beautys white we see; And joy, which is inseparate from these eyes, Stella now learns (strange case!) to weep in thee. Love moves thy pain, and like a faithful page, As thy looks stir, runs up and down, to make All folks prest at thy will thy pain to assuage; Nature with care sweats for her darlings sake, Knowing worlds pass, ere she enough can find Of such heaven stuff, to clothe so heavenly mind.

Thou art my lute, by thee I sing, My being is attuned to thee. Thou settest all my words a-wing, And meltest me to melody. Thou art my life, by thee I live, From thee proceed the joys I know; Sweetheart, thy hand has power to give The meed of lovethe cup of woe. Thou art my love, by thee I lead My soul the paths of light along, From vale to vale, from mead to mead, And home it in the hills of song. My song, my soul, my life, my all, Why need I pray or make my plea, Since my petition cannot fall; For Im already one with thee!

Thou art my lute, by thee I sing, my being a string tuned to thy voice. Thou settest my words aloft, meltest me to song, to flame, to flight. Thou art my life, by thee I breathe, from thee I draw the joy, the ache, the sweet, the stark. Sweetheart, thy hand, a wand, dispels the gloom, bestows the cup of love, the tear. Thou art my love, by thee I walk, my soul a pilgrim through the light, from valley to valley, from mead to mead, home to the hills where song is born. My song, my soul, my life, my all—why pray? Why plead? For I am one with thee, fused, aflame, eternal.

Perspective remains unyielding in their gaze, preserving the docile mandate of spring that merges March with the desolate splendor of Antarctic skies. These beings are but cattle, unseeing beyond the verdant expanse of grass and the pristine whiteness of snow, their inner essence enshrined in the radiance they neglect to bestow upon the transient rhythms of season. They are cumbersome, ponderous, and unflinching, while we, who turn the cider mill, savor the bitter tang of friendships, their acidic wine slowing our pulse, their shifting barbs (until the jest becomes too sharp to be kind) boast a considerable faith in others, believing ourselves capable of confronting the most whimsical specter. Above them, Old Mizzentop, a palatial white hostelry, its floors stacked with stoic height, its ceilings adorned with portholes and five-foil dormers, gazes through long tiers of windows toward the past.

We, who press the cider mill, sipping the bright, sharp sting of friendship's wine, our retarding phlegm, our shifting quarrels—when will the jest be too sharp to be kind? We boast much of our faith in others, yet we, too, could stalk down the merriest ghost. Care for thy soul as thing of greatest price, Made to the end to taste of power divine, Devoid of guilt, abhorring sin and vice, Apt by Gods grace to virtue to incline. Care for it so as by thy retchless train It be not brought to taste eternal pain. Care for thy corse, but chiefly for souls sake; Cut off excess, sustaining food is best; To vanquish pride but comely clothing take; Seek after skill, deep ignorance detest. Care so, I say, the flesh to feed and clothe That thou harm not thy soul and body both. Care for the world to do thy body right; Rack not thy wit to win thy wicked ways; Seek not to oppress the weak by wrongful might; To pay thy due do banish all delays. Care to dispend according to thy store, And in like sort be mindful of the poor. Care for thy soul, as for thy chiefest stay; Care for thy body for thy souls avail; Care for the world for bodys help alway; Care yet but so as virtue may prevail. Care in such sort that thou be sure of this: Care keep thee not from heaven and heavenly bliss.

Tend to the soul as the most precious artifact, forged to partake in the divine potency, stripped of moral blemish, averse to vice, and inclined by divine grace toward virtue. Nurture it with unflinching fidelity, lest it be led into the abyss of eternal anguish. Attend to the body, yet with greater devotion to the soul’s welfare; trim superfluous indulgence, sustenance most noble; subdue pride, don modest garb; pursue mastery, detest profound ignorance. Feed and clothe the flesh with such care that neither soul nor body be harmed. Tend the world to serve the body’s needs; do not strain the mind to pursue base ends; refrain from oppressing the weak through unjust force; discharge thy obligations without delay. Spend according to thy means, and in like measure attend to the destitute. Tend the soul, as its primary support; tend the body, for the soul’s benefit; tend the world, for the body’s aid; yet always with the intent that virtue may prevail. Care in such a way that thou art certain: care shall not bar thee from heaven or the bliss of the divine.

Care for thy soul, that sacred, burning flame, a treasure more than gold, made to drink deep of divine power, clean of sin, hating vice, yearning for grace to lift it high. Guard it so that no bitter grief may cling to it, no eternal wound be carved in its heart. Care for thy corpse, but chiefly for the soul's sake; trim excess, feed with what is best, wear clothes that please, and chase skill, despising deep ignorance. Feed and clothe the flesh with care, so that soul and body both may not be harmed. Care for the world to give thy body its due; let not thy mind be strained to gain wicked things; do not oppress the weak with false might; pay thy debts, and let no delay be thine. Spend according to what thou hast, and in like sort, be kind to the poor. Care for thy soul, thy chiefest hope; care for thy body, for the soul's good; care for the world, for the body's aid; care yet, but so that virtue may prevail. Care in such a way that thou art sure of this: care keeps thee from heaven and heavenly bliss.

Tend to the soul as the most precious artifact, forged to partake in the divine potency, stripped of moral blemish, averse to vice, and inclined by divine grace toward virtue. Feed and clothe the flesh with such care that neither soul nor body be harmed. Tend the world to serve the body’s needs; do not strain the mind to pursue base ends; refrain from oppressing the weak through unjust force; discharge thy obligations without delay. Spend according to thy means, and in like measure attend to the destitute. Care in such a way that thou art certain: care shall not bar thee from heaven or the bliss of the divine.

Time, that solitary architect of my disquiet, hath bestowed upon me a love once destined for bliss. How cruel thou art, O Time, who first anointed my soul with life, yet now turns my joy to ash? I question not my own negligence, but thy merciless haste—have I forsaken a single rite of devotion, or hast thou, in thy swift passage, left me to wander in the shadow of thy wrath? No moment shall I witness, where my happiness is most assured, save those now lost to thy relentless tide. Blame not my folly, but thy own cruelty—time hath given time only to be cursed. True love, unyielding, seeks no ends but its own; unworthy love, in contrast, pretends to worth, yet proves nothing. Therefore, O Time, cease thy merciless flight, and let me once more bask in the blessed realm of thy grace. Let me taste pleasure, let me rejoice in love, let me preserve faith, and let me ascend on the wings of fame. Never shall thy glory fade, unless it be undone by thy own undoing. For time, once lent, is a gain that never ends; and so, in thy name, let joy be what thou givest.

Sweet shades why doe you seeke to give delight To mee who deeme delight in this vilde place Butt torment, sorrow, and mine owne disgrace To taste of joy, or your vaine pleasing sight; Show them your pleasures who saw never night Of greife, wher joyings fauning, smiling face Appeers as day, wher griefe found never space Yett for a sigh, a grone, or envies spite; Butt O on mee a world of woes doe ly, Or els on mee all harmes strive to rely, And to attend like servants bound to mee, Heat in desire, while frosts of care I prove, Wanting my love, yett surfett doe with love Burne, and yett freeze, better in hell to bee.

Sweet shades, why do you seek to give delight  
To me who dwell in this desolate place,  
Where torment, sorrow, and my own disgrace  
Would taste of joy, or your vain, false light?  
Show them your pleasures, those who ne’er knew night  
Of grief, where joy’s false face, a fleeting smile,  
Appears as day, where sorrow found no trail—  
Yet for a sigh, a groan, or envy’s spite.  
But O, a world of woes lies heavy on me,  
Or else all harms rely on me to be,  
And serve me bound, with heat of desire,  
While care’s cold frost I bear, I prove.  
Desiring love, yet love burns, then freezes—  
Better in hell to be.

Whoso list to hunt, I know where is an hind, But as for me, helas, I may no more. The vain travail hath wearied me so sore, I am of them that farthest cometh behind. Yet may I by no means my wearied mind Draw from the deer, but as she fleeth afore Fainting I follow. I leave off therefore, Sithens in a net I seek to hold the wind. Who list her hunt, I put him out of doubt, As well as I may spend his time in vain. And graven with diamonds in letters plain There is written, her fair neck round about: Noli me tangere, for Caesar's I am, And wild for to hold, though I seem tame.

He who seeks the chase shall find the doe, yet I, alas, am bound to cease. The futile toil has drained me to the core, I am of those who lag far behind. Yet I may not sever my weary mind from the deer, but as she fleets ahead, I falter and follow. I therefore desist, since in a net I strive to ensnare the wind. He who seeks her hunt, I make him clear, as well as I may waste his time in futility. Graven in diamonds, plain as letters, there is written round her fair neck: "Noli me tangere," for I am Caesar's, wild to hold, though I seem tame.

My true-love hath my heart and I have his, By just exchange one for the other given: I hold his dear, and mine he cannot miss; There never was a bargain better driven. His heart in me keeps me and him in one; My heart in him his thoughts and senses guides: He loves my heart, for once it was his own; I cherish his because in me it bides. His heart his wound received from my sight; My heart was wounded with his wounded heart; For as from me on him his hurt did light, So still, methought, in me his hurt did smart: Both equal hurt, in this change sought our bliss, My true love hath my heart and I have his.

My true love and I have exchanged our hearts in a transaction of equal worth, each claiming the other as its own. His heart resides within me, binding us in a singular, unbroken unity; mine dwells within him, directing his will and sense. He cherishes my heart, for it was once his; I hold his dear, as it now resides in me. His heart bears the wound I could not see, while mine is wounded by the pain of his; as light from me has touched him, so too does his affliction find its echo in me. In this mutual suffering, our bliss is found—a balance of shared torment, a symphony of reciprocal loss, where love is not possession, but a reciprocal exchange of souls. My true love hath my heart and I have his.

My true love and I have exchanged our hearts in a transaction of equal worth, each claiming the other as its own. His heart resides within me, binding us in a singular, unbroken unity; mine dwells within him, directing his will and sense. He cherishes my heart, for it was once his; I hold his dear, as it now resides in me. His heart bears the wound I could not see, while mine is wounded by the pain of his; as light from me has touched him, so too does his affliction find its echo in me. In this mutual suffering, our bliss is found—a balance of shared torment, a symphony of reciprocal loss, where love is not possession, but a reciprocal exchange of souls. My true love hath my heart and I have his.

Both hearts, both wounds, in this switch found their sweet peace—my true love holds my heart, and I have his.

Farewell friend wantcatcher, since 'twill not be, Thou cannot catch the wants, but they catch me.

I traversed the fields as a wantcatcher, spotting one who claimed to seize desires. I approached, eager to witness his mastery. "Have you captured wants?" I asked. He affirmed, presenting a dozen recently secured. "None remain?" I pressed. "None," he replied. I then revealed the paradox: the more one seeks, the more is found. Yet his labor proved futile, for desires had already infiltrated my purse. Farewell, friend wantcatcher; you cannot capture wants, but they capture you.

Now in the West the slender moon lies low, And now Orion glimmers through the trees, Clearing the earth with even pace and slow, And now the stately-moving Pleiades, In that soft infinite darkness overhead Hang jewel-wise upon a silver thread. And all the lonelier stars that have their place, Calm lamps within the distant southern sky, And planet-dust upon the edge of space, Look down upon the fretful world, and I Look up to outer vastness unafraid And see the stars which sang when earth was made.

Now in the West, the moon hangs thin and low, Orion glimmers through the trees, clearing the earth with slow, even pace. The Pleiades move stately above, jewel-wise on a silver thread in that soft, infinite dark. All the lonelier stars, calm lamps in the southern sky, and planet-dust at the edge of space, watch the fretful world. I look up, unafraid, and see the stars that sang when earth was made.

Potuia, potuia White grave goddess, Pity my sadness, O silence of Paros. I am not of these about thy feet, These garments and decorum; I am thy brother, Thy lover of aforetime crying to thee, And thou hearest me not. I have whispered thee in thy solitudes Of our loves in Phrygia, The far ecstasy of burning noons When the fragile pipes Ceased in the cypress shade, And the brown fingers of the shepherd Moved over slim shoulders; And only the cicada sang. I have told thee of the hills And the lisp of reeds And the sun upon thy breasts, And thou hearest me not, Potuia, potuia Thou hearest me not.

I have told thee of the hills and the lisp of reeds and the sun upon thy breasts, and thou hearest me not, Potuia, Potuia, thou hearest me not.

Potuia, Potuia—White grave goddess, pity my sadness, O silence of Paros. I am not of these about thy feet, these garments and decorum; I am thy brother, thy lover of aforetime crying to thee, and thou hearest me not. I have whispered thee in thy solitudes of our loves in Phrygia, the far ecstasy of burning noons when the fragile pipes ceased in the cypress shade, and the brown fingers of the shepherd moved over slim shoulders; and only the cicada sang. I have told thee of the hills and the lisp of reeds and the sun upon thy breasts, and thou hearest me not, Potuia, Potuia—thou hearest me not.
